title: NFC South Week 10 Review: Carolina takes the lead (for now)
summary: The Panthers and Saints faced off for the division lead in what was one of the worst-officiated games this decade, while the Falcons tried to keep pace with the Chiefs. The Buccaneers had the week off, and fans across the league appreciated seeing one less NFC South team play. Here’s the Week 10 NFC South […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 15: New Orleans Saints defensive players huddle in the second half of a game against the Carolina Panthers at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Morgan Simmons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Panthers and Saints faced off for the division lead in what was one of the worst-officiated games this decade, while the Falcons tried to keep pace with the Chiefs. The Buccaneers had the week off, and fans across the league appreciated seeing one less NFC South team play. Here’s the Week 10 NFC South Review. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) Week 10 Result: Bye Week Week 11 Opponent: Detroit Lions The Buccaneers were on the bye, and they desperately needed it. Tampa Bay was hoping to get some good rest, but it appears Baker Mayfield is dealing with a foot injury that’s bad enough that the team felt like it needed to sign Cooper Rush. I had no idea Rush was a podiatrist, but I’m glad he can find work. Like every team in this division, the Buccaneers are not out of the title race. They’ll need a near-spotless finish to win the division, and they have a tough start on the road in Detroit. Carolina Panthers (4-5) Week 10 Result: Panthers 20 – Saints 17 Week 11 Opponent: Baltimore Ravens The Cardiac Cats pulled out the win in the final seconds of this division matchup against the Saints . It was an ugly game for the most part; 20 of the 37 total points were scored in the 4th quarter. Chuba Hubbard led the way on the ground, scoring the Panthers two touchdowns of the game. Young struggled to complete just over 50% of his passes for 200 yards, but he played a turnover-free game, and that’s what it takes to win a slugfest. Carolina sits atop the division and will host the Ravens next week. Ryan Fitzgerald wins it for Carolina! pic.twitter.com/Ry9bbQQkWv — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 New Orleans Saints (3-6) Week 10 Result: Saints 17 – Panthers 20 Week 11 Opponent: Chicago Bears The Saints couldn’t build on their Week 9 win and added another L to their record. Kellen Moore’s offense is out of sorts. Tyler Shough finished another game as the team’s leading rusher, with only 25 yards. The Saints defense had one of their better performances of the season but couldn’t stop the Panthers when it counted. Things could be worse; they could be last in the division, but that’s not a very high bar. There’s no rest for the wicked; the Saints will travel to Chicago to take on the Monster of the Midway. Atlanta Falcons (3-7) Week 10 Result: Falcons 13 – Chiefs 35 Week 11 Opponent: Bye Week The Falcons got torched by Patrick Mahomes and have the longest active losing streak in the division. Michael Penix has been stuck in a rut for weeks, and the team has been unable to get him out of it. The offense can’t stop committing penalties or turning the ball over. The team had 18 last year; they have 19 and counting this season. The defense is coming apart at the seams and can’t stop the run or the pass right now. The bye week couldn’t have come at a better time, and they’ll need the extra prep because Brian Flores will be waiting for them. Patrick Mahomes throws FIVE touchdowns in a game for the first time since September 2022. 22/33, 348 PASS YDS, 5 TD, 0 INT vs Falcons. Less than a year after tearing his ACL and LCL, Mahomes is making a serious case for Comeback Player of the Year. https://t.co/MyEEYMU0x1 pic.twitter.com/qQbQObcoQl — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 15, 2026 It’s looking more and more like 7 wins will get the job done this year, which means it’s still anyone’s title for the taking. Some teams should probably face the reality that winning the South won’t help their futures, but that wouldn’t be any fun.

title: Winners and losers from the Ravens’ Week 10 loss to the Chargers
summary: The Ravens suffered their fifth straight loss in Week 10, giving the Chargers their first win of the season. There were a few bright spots in Baltimore’s loss, including the debut of a new quarterback, but plenty of blame to be handed out as well. Winners Jacoby Brissett: The Ravens’ newest quarterback was thrown straight […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Mark Andrews #89 of the Baltimore Ravens reacts against the Los Angeles Chargers during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens suffered their fifth straight loss in Week 10, giving the Chargers their first win of the season. There were a few bright spots in Baltimore’s loss, including the debut of a new quarterback, but plenty of blame to be handed out as well. Winners Jacoby Brissett: The Ravens’ newest quarterback was thrown straight into the fire, dropping back 51 times in his debut. While it was not a perfect performance, Brissett proved that he can operate Baltimore’s offense at a high enough level to remain competitive. The veteran journeyman flashed a connection with multiple Ravens pass catchers after being with the team only 10 days. Staying alive for a potential Lamar Jackson return down the road seems like wishful thinking after losing to an 0-8 team and falling to 4-6, but Brissett at least elevates Baltimore’s offense to a watchable status for the fans who will continue to show up. Mark Andrews: It was reported during the game that Andrews had broken his hand earlier in the season, which could explain some of the veteran tight end’s struggles this year. Andrews looked more like his old self against Los Angeles, leading the team with eight catches for 82 yards and an 87.4 grade from Pro Football Focus — all season-highs, too. Brissett seemed to have immediate chemistry with Andrews, so his production could continue to improve for the remainder of the season. Mike Green: Green was the standout on the Ravens’ defense with perhaps the best game of his career. The second-year edge rusher had the team’s only two sacks against Justin Herbert while also making several plays in the run game. Green now leads the team in sacks for the season with 5.5. Marlon Humphrey: On a defense full of highly-paid underperforming players this season, Humphrey has taken perhaps the most criticism of all. The former All-Pro showed up against the Chargers, however, leading the defense with an 82.4 PFF grade. Although it was recovered by Los Angeles, Humphrey forced a fumble on the Chargers’ first drive of the game by stripping running back Omarion Hampton. Josh Cuevas : The rookie tight end caught three passes for 37 yards, all coming during a two-minute drill drive to get a field goal before halftime. Losers Offensive line: Baltimore’s offensive line has been under fire this season, and for good reason. The unit was unable to generate anything on the ground against Los Angeles as the offense finished with an abysmal 16 yards on 15 total carries. Derrick Henry was hit in the backfield on what felt like every handoff, while the best run of the night, a 14-yard gain by Justice Hill, was nullified due to a holding penalty. Ja’Kobi Lane: Of his team-high 11 targets, Lane came down with only three catches for 61 yards. The third-round rookie was the intended target on Brissett’s interception, though the pass was slightly behind him. Lane’s biggest blunder of the night was dropping a potential touchdown just before halftime. The Ravens had to settle for a field goal instead in a game that ultimately came down to three points. Zay Flowers: The fourth-year wideout put the nail in the coffin for Baltimore with a costly fumble at the end of the game. Down by three with over two minutes left in the game, the Ravens’ offense was driving before Flowers was stripped after a 15-yard catch. His five lost fumbles since entering the league are tied for the most among wide receivers during that time. Derrick Henry: It is hard to fault Henry too much for his struggles this season with how often he has been hit in the backfield on run plays, but the future Hall of Famer still deserves some blame. Even when getting past the line of scrimmage without being hit, Henry has not shown the same ability to break tackles or make defenders miss this season. While he did reach the end zone twice against the Chargers, Henry finished the night with just 20 yards on 10 rushing attempts and only 10 yards on five receptions. Jesse Minter: Rookie head coaches deserve a grace period, especially when their team loses its MVP quarterback, but the heat may be turning up on Minter after 10 weeks. Baltimore’s defense was supposed to rebound with Minter at the helm, but the unit has been just as bad, if not worse than last season, with an improved group of players. A lack of discipline has been a major issue for the team overall, with penalties still being a weekly talking point. The players perhaps deserve the brunt of the blame, but the head coach is ultimately the one responsible for the product fielded every week.

title: Ravens discussion: what changes should Jesse Minter make going forward?
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are headed in the wrong direction. General manager Eric DeCosta will be responsible for the roster reset that should come this offseason, but it’s up to head coach Jesse Minter to stop the skid down the stretch. Today, let’s discuss what changes Minter needs to make for the rest of the season. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - NOVEMBER 05: Head coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens looks on during the second half against the Jacksonville Jaguars at M&T Bank Stadium on November 5, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are headed in the wrong direction. General manager Eric DeCosta will be responsible for the roster reset that should come this offseason, but it’s up to head coach Jesse Minter to stop the skid down the stretch. Today, let’s discuss what changes Minter needs to make for the rest of the season. Your answer may depend on your outlook. Optimists will look for ways to keep winning games, pessimists will call for immediate overhauls. Here are my thoughts; be sure to add yours in the comments section below! Nikhil’s take: The company line out of The Castle will remain the same: keep playoff hopes alive and hope Lamar Jackson can save the season. That seems exceedingly unlikely at this point. And here’s the thing: wholesale changes looking towards the future aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive with being more competitive. If, for example, the Ravens still think Carson Vinson can be their future left tackle, he could rotate in with Ronnie Stanley, who has struggled in his own right. Elimination from playoff contention should give Vinson the starting job for the rest of the year. The front office also needs to have an uncomfortable conversation about Roquan Smith’s future in Baltimore. There’s a growing argument that Trenton Simpson could be the Ravens’ future at inside linebacker on a more mid-level contract – or a bigger move back to the 80/20 approach of years past. That would indicate Buchanan paired with a veteran – perhaps Smith for one more year or a cheap offseason acquisition – could be the long-term plan. Cornerback Marlon Humphrey and tight end Mark Andrews both had bounce-back games vs. the Chargers, so calls for their benching will likely cease. Still, the Ravens should continue to work in T.J. Tampa and rookies Matt Hibner and Josh Cuevas. Getting third-round rookie Ja’Kobi Lane more opportunities – even after a tough showing on Monday night – is a must, and seeing what Devontez Walker and Elijah Sarratt can do isn’t a bad idea, either. Now, it’s your turn! What should Minter change for the rest of the season? Let us know in the comments section below!

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 10: Run defense and run offense crater in fifth straight loss
summary: Offense Jacoby Brissett’s debut with the Ravens saw him play every offensive snap (69). He appeared to suffer a knee injury in the first quarter but shook it off and missed no plays. The entire starting offensive line also went the distance with the exception of Vega Ioane, who departed after 36 snaps due to […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Jacoby Brissett #11 and Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens warm up prior to the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Offense QB: Jacoby Brissett 69 RB: Derrick Henry 38, Justice Hill 33 WR: Rashod Bateman 63, Zay Flowers 61, Ja’Kobi Lane 44, Chris Moore 6, Devontez Walker 3, LaJohntay Wester 1 TE: Mark Andrews 40, Matthew Hibner 22, Nick Vannett 14, Josh Cuevas 11 OL: Ronnie Stanley 69, John Simpson 69, Cam Jurgens 69, Roger Rosengarten 69, Vega Ioane 36, Chuma Edoga 33, Carson Vinson 9 Jacoby Brissett’s debut with the Ravens saw him play every offensive snap (69). He appeared to suffer a knee injury in the first quarter but shook it off and missed no plays. The entire starting offensive line also went the distance with the exception of Vega Ioane, who departed after 36 snaps due to a shoulder injury. Practice squad call-up Chuma Edoga replaced him at right guard for the final 33 offensive plays. The running back split saw Derrick Henry play 38 snaps to Justice Hill’s 33 snaps. Henry was rendered ineffective by the Los Angeles Chargers’ defensive front, gaining just 10 rushing yards on 10 carries. The Ravens once again struggled to get any push in the running game and open up lanes. Mark Andrews had his best game of the season in a position-high 40 snaps, catching eight passes for 82 receiving yards — both of which led the team. Despite playing only 11 snaps, Josh Cuevas was the only other tight end to catch a pass. He had three receptions for 37 yards. Matthew Hibner and Nick Vannett were not targeted. It was a three-man show at wide receiver, where Rashod Bateman surprisingly out-snapped Zay Flowers slightly (63 to 61). Flowers had six receptions for 74 yards but lost a crucial fumble late in the fourth quarter with the Ravens threatening to tie the game or take the lead. Bateman caught three passes for 42 yards. Ja’Kobi Lane continues to operate as the clear No. 3 wideout and saw the most targets on the team (11). He caught three balls for 61 yards, but dropped a costly third-down pass that would have set up a first-and-goal. Defense DL: Travis Jones 43, Broderick Washington 32, Calais Campbell 28, Nnamdi Madubuike 28, John Jenkins 10 EDGE: Mike Green 45, Trey Hendrickson 41, Zion young 15, Ethan Burke 13 ILB: Roquan Smith 57, Trenton Simpson 47, Teddye Buchanan 5 CB: Nate Wiggins 53, Marlon Humphrey 42, Keyon Martin 18, Chidobe Awuzie 16, T.J. Tampa 3 S: Kyle Hamilton 56, Malaki Starks 54, K’Von Wallace 11, Keondre Jackson 10 Nnamdi Madubuike left the game early with a hamstring injury after 28 snaps, which opened the door for Broderick Washington to play elevated snaps (32). Travis Jones led all defensive linemen with 43 snaps and Calais Campbell had two quarterback hits in his 28 snaps. The Ravens struggled to defend the run, as they allowed 160 rushing yards and the Chargers averaged 4.7 yards per carry with two touchdowns. On the edge, Mike Green’s 45 snaps saw him wreak havoc with four solo tackles, two sacks, two tackles for loss and three quarterback hits. Green has been the team’s most effective sack-getter this season. Trey Hendrickson played 41 snaps but had just one tackle with no sacks or quarterback hits. Zion Young and Ethan Burke each saw a big reduction in playing time. Roquan Smith was the lone defender to play 100% of snaps. Trenton Simpson was on the field for all but 10 plays alongside him, recording eight tackles, two quarterback hits and a tackle for loss. Teddye Buchanan’s playing time continue to be minimal, as he played just five snaps. Kyle Hamilton left the field for one play to be checked for a concussion but quickly returned. Malaki Starks played 54 snaps, while the backup safeties combined to take on 21 snaps. At cornerback, Marlon Humphrey was on the sidelines at times but did not see a huge reduction in playing time as he finished with 42 snaps. Nate Wiggins was nearly on the field for every down, Chidobe Awuzie only played 16 snaps on the outside. T.J. Tampa reverted back to a minimal defensive role (three snaps) and Keyon Martin’s 18 snaps were the third most at the position.

title: Buffalo Bills trending up, trending down: Bills beat Jets, and Dolphins come next
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 31-12, and the defense that closed the game deserves most of the credit. With a second divisional matchup in sight, Miami is 1-8 and has lost three straight, and Buffalo is favored by 16.5 according to SI’s betting preview. The record hides a defense that has allowed […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 31-12, and the defense that closed the game deserves most of the credit. With a second divisional matchup in sight, Miami is 1-8 and has lost three straight, and Buffalo is favored by 16.5 according to SI’s betting preview. The record hides a defense that has allowed 320.5 yards per game, the 10th fewest in the NFL, while facing one of the toughest schedules of opposing offenses. That is the group the Bills will see on Sunday, and here are the players who can make the difference for Buffalo: Keep It Up T.J. Parker, outside linebacker Parker had two sacks on consecutive plays early in the fourth quarter and five pressures on 26 pass-rush snaps, per PFF. He is the first Bills rookie with two or more sacks in a game since Greg Rousseau did it against Miami in 2021, and he now has 3.5 on the season. He played more than half the defensive snaps and made the most of his opportunities. Miami’s line has given up 24 sacks on Malik Willis, and in Week 10 the Colts credited 8 pressures and 3 sacks on Kyle McCord, who was making his first NFL start. With McCord most likely under center again, a fast rusher who wins early is exactly the problem he does not want. DJ Moore, wide receiver Moore finished with four catches for 90 yards and a 45-yard touchdown, plus a 32-yard catch on a crossing route. His 75.1 PFF grade was one of the five best on offense. The Dolphins play rookies at a higher rate than any defense in the league, and cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe have played every defensive snap since Week 7. Taaffe has three interceptions, and Johnson returned one for a 59-yard touchdown against Indianapolis. A veteran who finds space against young defensive backs is what Buffalo needs against a ball-hawking secondary. Moore should find opportunities to haul in another big play or two if Joe Brady gives him the opportunity to capitalize deep again. Terrel Bernard, linebacker After taking heavy criticism following a rough 2025 season (48.8 PFF grade, 73rd of 88 linebackers) and a 39.9 grade in Week 5, Terrel Bernard deserves real credit for his recent turnaround. Over the last two weeks, he has totaled 14 tackles, two passes defended, an interception, and zero missed tackles against the Jets — highlighted by a 72.5 PFF grade in Week 10 and a massive, clean hit that knocked Geno Smith out of the game. That surge has boosted his season grade to 66.6 (29th of 82) with a 65.0 coverage mark and an 80.9 passer rating allowed. Buffalo will need that version of Bernard on Sunday to anchor the middle against Miami’s Ollie Gordon II — who just posted 100 yards against Minnesota and 88 against Cincinnati — and contain quarterback Kyle McCord (17-of-32, 209 yards vs. Indianapolis), who thrives on quick, underneath throws. Step Up James Cook, running back (In the passing game ) Hear me out. Cook ran for 157 yards at 8.7 per carry against the Jets, and the run game is not the issue. The receiving side is. Through Week 10, he has 12 catches on 19 targets for 110 yards, with two drops according to Pro Football Reference, and an average depth of target of -0.2 yards. In Week 9, he failed to bring in his only target against Minnesota. Josh Allen said publicly that he needs to take more checkdowns, but we know that’s not his favorite kind of throw. When he decides to settle for it, seeing his running back not getting the job done makes that harder. Cook is leaving receiving production on the table in a role that fits him. This offense can be way more dangerous if he can take advantage of those more often. Honorable Mentions Keep It Up Khalil Shakir, wide receiver: The highest PFF grade on the offense (77.6) came on two catches for 26 yards, three rushes for 29, and an 80.3 blocking grade. His short-game work is what to watch against a young secondary that tackles well. Spencer Brown, right tackle: Brown did not practice early in the week and was doubtful, yet played and allowed no pressures on 13 reps against Jets rookie David Bailey, per Next Gen Stats. Bailey came into the game with 40 pressures on 194 pass-rush attempts (20.6%). His PFF grade was 75.3. Chop Robinson is a different test, but Brown showed he can handle a top young rusher. Dalton Kincaid, tight end: His 54-yard catch started the second half, and he earned a 73.1 PFF grade. Miami’s rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez has played 99.3 percent of the defensive snaps, using Kincaid over the middle is a matchup to test the rookie in coverage. Step Up Dawson Knox, tight end: One catch for 7 yards on three targets, a 41.2 PFF grade (the lowest of any offensive player on the team) and a 51.1 run-blocking grade. His best game of the year came a week earlier: four catches on five targets for 37 yards. Buffalo needs that level of play against Miami’s linebackers. T.J. Sanders, defensive tackle: A 39.6 PFF grade. Miami has leaned on Gordon, so the interior has to hold up. After a promising start to his season, he hasn’t played well as his role diminished with Ed Oliver back. Jordan Hancock, cornerback: A 43.7 PFF grade. With Christian Benford, Max Hairston, and Dee Alford banged up, more of the secondary will fall on him. He has to make the most of his opportunities, especially with how well Te’Cory Couch played in his last game. Final Thoughts The Jets game showed a defense that punishes opposing QBs and an offense that was grounded for most of the first half, but had an extra gear to make up for it in the second. Miami, 1-8 and starting a rookie quarterback, is the kind of opponent that they can’t allow to give them trouble. Parker, Moore, and Bernard have the best case to build on Sunday, and Cook and Chubb have the clearest chance to change the story. Which of this week’s Step Up names do you think responds best against Miami? Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: Examining Buffalo Bills run heaviness in first half of 2026 season
summary: The Buffalo Bills have loved running the football thus far in the 2026 season. James Cook has the second-most carries in the NFL right now at 187. As a team, the Bills are the current owners of the second-highest first-down designed run rate in the NFL at 61.3%. Now, sure, the Bills have recently played […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills have loved running the football thus far in the 2026 season. James Cook has the second-most carries in the NFL right now at 187. As a team, the Bills are the current owners of the second-highest first-down designed run rate in the NFL at 61.3%. Now, sure, the Bills have recently played in a collection of games that featured plenty of garbage time, when Buffalo has attempted to burn clock by tapping into the run game. Even when garbage-time is considered, the Bills have the NFL’s second-highest run rate on all downs at 45.7%. The rest of the league averages a designed run play on 39.3%. Quarterback scrambles — that occur on dropbacks — and spikes and kneels are excluded in that calculation. Analytics have proven that passing the football is more efficient than running the football. And this article isn’t going to show that the Bills have actually become more efficient on the ground than through the air. Right now, in non-garbage time situations, Buffalo’s designed-run game has provided the team +0.023 EPA per play, the eighth-highest figure in the NFL. The team’s pass game has provided the team +0.239 EPA per dropback, the fourth-best in football. Unsurprisingly, the difference in value added for each method of moving the football has been seismic. Up until now, the Bills have genuinely attempted to “establish” the run in their first nine games of the 2026 campaign. Accepting that fact raises two questions: what type of play call have the Bills chosen on second down and how effective have their second downs been? Before I begin with the results, despite an overall negative EPA in first-down run scenarios (-0.059, the 15th-highest in football), the Bills have had 16.4% of those runs gain 10+ yards. That’s the fourth-best in the NFL and much higher than the league average of 10.3%. This is where things get fascinating for Buffalo’s elite offense. And where it has leaned on its pass game. On second down after a first-down run — in non-garbage time scenarios, of course — the Bills have dropped back to pass 73.8% of the time, which is the fourth-highest rate in the NFL and noticeably higher than the league average of 64.5%. On all second downs, regardless of whether a run or pass was called on first down, the Bills’ dropback rate is 66.9%, the ninth-highest in the NFL. While the Bills are actually below league average in conventional passing statistics within both second-down parameters, they are 12th in EPA per dropback in second downs after a first down run and on all non-garbage time second downs. An enormous element of said impressive EPA per dropback on second down for the Bills despite below-average passing statistics in those situations is of course Josh Allen scrambles, the ultimately luxury built into Buffalo’s dropback game. The possibility of an Allen scramble occurring on a dropback must be considered. Allen has eight scrambles on second-down runs that have totaled 87 yards. That’s 10.9 yards per scramble, the second-highest average among all quarterbacks in those scenarios. His +1.162 EPA on those plays, is far and away, tops in the NFL. You have survived this massive number dump, and I appreciate you making it this far. Essentially, yes — the Bills have been very run heavy. But they’ve smartly morphed into being one of the league’s more pass-happy clubs on second down, and Allen’s running on second-down dropbacks have been incredibly effective.

title: Buffalo Bills recent adds to roster have provided value
summary: Sometimes, important additions to an NFL team don’t occur until close to September… or even in-season. On August 18, after their first preseason game, the Bills signed veteran defensive lineman Greg Gaines — potentially as a response to rookie defensive tackle Zane Durant being injured late in the opening exhibition game against the Panthers. Almost […]
full_text: Sometimes, important additions to an NFL team don’t occur until close to September… or even in-season. On August 18, after their first preseason game, the Bills signed veteran defensive lineman Greg Gaines — potentially as a response to rookie defensive tackle Zane Durant being injured late in the opening exhibition game against the Panthers. Almost exactly two weeks later, on the last day of August, as the team seemingly had no clear-cut candidate to return punts, Buffalo scooped up Greg Dortch after he was surprisingly cut by the Lions. Through the first nine games of the season, both have provided valuable, low-key contributions to this Bills team. On the surface, Gaines’ presence has been irrelevant. He has 11 tackles and one tackles for loss along with two pressures on 77 pass-rush snaps on 22.5% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps. But when Gaines is on the field, he’s a magnet for blockers, which has a massive ripple effect on his teammates. More blockers on him, fewer on other Bills defenders. Gaines is currently 10th in the NFL among qualifying defensive linemen in double-team rate (67.5%) on pass-rush snaps. It’s the highest rate on Buffalo’s roster right now (among qualifiers). As for Dortch, the value he’s added has been easier to discern. Among punt returners with at least 15 returns to date, his 9.2 yards-per-return average is seventh-best in the NFL. He’s been darn good as a kicker returner too, so teams aren’t able to simply directionally kick it away from reigning All-Pro kicker returner Ray Davis. While Davis is second in the NFL in average kick-return yardage at 29.6 entering Week 11, Dortch is tied for 12th with an average of 27.2 yards per kick return. And he’s actually returned nearly double the amount of kickoffs (23) as Davis (12). And then there’s Amani Hooker. Of course, the jury is still out on how much the trade-deadline acquisition will impact Buffalo’s defense. But in his first game, after a week of practice in a new scheme on a new team, he played the most defensive snaps of any Bills defender (70), made seven tackles, and had a pass breakup that was nearly an interception. Hooker will play a full-time role at free safety the rest of the way. Gaines and Dortch have proven to be savvy, low-cost additions by the Bills close to the start of the regular season. These adds have become the embodiment of Brandon Beane’s often cited perpetual pursuit of improving the roster.

(Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills announced a series of roster moves as they begin preparations to host the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium for Week 11. Buffalo has signed defensive back Te’Cory Couch to the practice squad, bringing him back to One Bills Drive after being released ahead of last weekend’s game and once he cleared waivers Monday afternoon. The 27-year-old defender out of the University of Miami has played in four games for Buffalo this season. In those games, Couch has made eight tackles (6 solo), showcasing a knack for limiting big plays after the catch with solid tackling. Couch joined the Bills in 2024, entering the NFL as an undrafted rookie free agent. To make room for Couch, Buffalo once again parted ways with veteran offensive guard Nick Broeker, who has been re-added to the team’s practice squad several times already this season. Broeker has yet to appear in a regular-season game for the Bills, though he has previously played in 12 games (2023 and 2024 seasons) for the Denver Broncos. Broeker was originally drafted by Buffalo in Round 7 (230th overall) of the 2023 NFL Draft. The Bills also announced that rookie offensive guard Ar’maj Reed-Adams has been placed on Injured Reserve, which will sideline him for at least the next four games. With Reed-Adams heading to IR, that opens up a spot on Buffalo’s 53-man roster. A potential candidate to take over that roster opening is veteran wide receiver Tyrell Shavers, whose return-to-practice window was recently opened as the next step toward a return to the field following a devastating knee injury against the Jacksonville Jaguars during the Bills’ 2025 NFL playoff run.

title: Jim Leonhard has embraced aggressiveness in Buffalo Bills defensive scheme since bye week
summary: Yes, the Buffalo Bills have gone from a gauntlet of high-level quarterbacks to start to the season to a consecutive collection of backups, and that drastic shift in competition has coincided with a drastic shift in defensive philosophy from Jim Leonhard. In the first six games of the 2026 season, when Buffalo’s defense was a […]
full_text: Yes, the Buffalo Bills have gone from a gauntlet of high-level quarterbacks to start to the season to a consecutive collection of backups, and that drastic shift in competition has coincided with a drastic shift in defensive philosophy from Jim Leonhard. In the first six games of the 2026 season, when Buffalo’s defense was a liability, the Bills played man coverage 16.4% of the time, per Fantasy Points Data. That was the 24th-highest man-coverage rate in the NFL. Also in those first six outings, Buffalo’s blitz rate was 27.9%, the 20th-highest blitz rate in football. Then the bye week happened. Since then, the Bills’ man-coverage rate jumped to 25.7%. In that three-game sample, that’s the 13th-highest in the league. Buffalo’s blitz rate has been 33.6% combined in Weeks 8, 9, and 10, the 13th-highest blitz rate in the NFL. (Can’t forget too — there was plenty of garbage time in all three contests, where the Bills, like any team, were prompted to sit back in soft zone to keep everything in front of them.) The new man-coverage and blitz rates don’t represent massive, 180-degree changes in philosophy. And we likely won’t be able to fully discern how much Leonhard’s man-coverage and blitzing movement post-bye has actually made the Bills defense better until Thanksgiving night against Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs. But one thing is for sure — Leonhard’s defense has recently started to look like what we expected Leonhard’s defense to look like all along.

title: Against the Jets, Buffalo Bills continue irritating penalty trend
summary: The Buffalo Bills not only beat the New York Jets, but they did so in pretty convincing fashion. There’s just one problem though. While many aspects of the game were entertaining, the Bills continue to be very annoying when it comes to flags. Namely; there’s nothing interesting to talk about for the second week in […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills not only beat the New York Jets, but they did so in pretty convincing fashion. There’s just one problem though. While many aspects of the game were entertaining, the Bills continue to be very annoying when it comes to flags. Namely; there’s nothing interesting to talk about for the second week in a row. Sure, they had ten flags total but not a single one is all that fun to discuss. For shame Buffalo! On a slightly more serious note however, this lack of “sexy” flags is part of a problem you might care about and that’s pre- and at-the-snap flags. Very avoidable, the frequency in which the Bills help out the opposition while they’re lining up is actually quite aggravating. I did make a video on one play though, as a “thank you” for dropping in. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts When I was picking the color scheme for the charts, I may have leaned into the Holiday theme as my favorite band just released the greatest Christmas song of all time . You’re welcome and Merry ****ing Christmas to ya! Oh right! Penalties. Yeah, both teams were pretty average. The Bills had a greater than average volume on thrown flags, but two declined and the one offset mitigated the damage. Penalty Yards When it comes to yards, here’s a major indicator of boring flags. Average counts and below average yardage lost. That typically means the penalties lean heavy towards procedural ones which I already told you they did. The Jets are about as expected. The slight elevation on the Jets’ True Yards isn’t even that far out of what with certain flag types able to wipe out large chunks of yards quite quickly as you’ll see in just a moment. Penalty Harm New York Jets The Jets had 11.8 Harm total, just a touch above our bad day cutoff of 10.0 Harm. This is largely on the back of some usual culprits. Namely offensive holding and defensive pass interference. The latter of which was assessed for 17 yards (so it does NOT contribute to the spike in True Yards above) and one down. For the offensive holding calls, one occurred on first down and the other was on special teams meaning all the extra Harm is negated yardage to the tune of 35 yards, or in other words the entirety of the spike in True Yards. The Jets at least have a little intrigue on their side of things with the items mentioned above. And they even spiced up one of their false starts with a rounding error. You don’t usually see a six-yarder for this but as long time readers know sometimes the way the ball is spotted the play-by-play rounds things and creates these errors. Buffalo Bills Just look at this foolishness. Of their ten flags, nine of them were pre- or at-the-snap ones. NINE! And two were pretty impactful all things considered. The obvious one is the illegal shift. That flag came on 3rd & 7 at midfield. The illegal shift wiped out a 16-yard gain. Now 3rd & 12, Allen tried to go deep and was picked off. Buffalo had essentially made it to field goal range if the pass was able to stand, but indirectly this ended the drive. Ed Oliver’s neutral zone infraction didn’t rate high on the Harm scale, but it gave the Jets new life. Rather than 4th & 6 and pretending to go for it, they decided to actually go for it on 4th & 1 and got it. A few plays later they got within field goal range and put up 25% of their scoring output for the day. Davison Igbinosun was the lone “not lining up poorly” flag so I figured I’d take a look to see if it was legitimate and also highlight the only one that could potentially have a decent story with it. Good eyes on the ref for seeing it, and the offsetting offensive holding flag was preeeeeetty obvious. pic.twitter.com/BpbOz1ftlK — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) November 17, 2026 Buffalo’s total Harm was 7.1 so not remotely a bad day. Just an irritating one.

title: Panthers vs Saints game review: Finally
summary: If there is only one thing in this world that can be said with certainty, it is that following and watching the Carolina Panthers is not for the faint of heart. One must be resolute in their fandom in order to withstand the trauma inflicted on those who tune in to see what Dave Canales […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 15: Head coach Dave Canales and Chuba Hubbard #30 of the Carolina Panthers celebrate after Hubbard's rushing touchdown in the second quarter of a game against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Wes Hale/Getty Images) | Getty Images If there is only one thing in this world that can be said with certainty, it is that following and watching the Carolina Panthers is not for the faint of heart. One must be resolute in their fandom in order to withstand the trauma inflicted on those who tune in to see what Dave Canales and boys in process blue have in store that week. I say this because had Sunday’s nail biter of match-up gone to overtime, I may not have survived. Not to say this would have been entirely the Panthers fault, as many of the aspects of the game that threatened my mortality were beyond their control. The main threat to my well being coming in the form of the little yellow flags that we all learned clash harshly with process blue. Yet, despite the fever dream of a broadcast that seemingly consisted of 80% penalty announcements and 20% turducken propaganda, the Panthers emerged victorious and gained sole control of the NFC South. Sure, you would like the win to be a little prettier and inspirational, but after losing three straight contests beggars cannot be choosers – and the Panthers were certainly begging for a win. Thankfully, the Panthers did more than just beg for the win. In fact, there’s been a few changes, both subtle and not subtle, that have been made in recent weeks that may have contributed to Sunday’s victory. For this game review, instead of rehashing the officiating debacle that we covered earlier this week let us instead focus on the details that allowed the Panthers to overcome it. Aggressiveness When Todd Wash took over as defensive coordinator, he did so with the promise that the Panthers would play more aggressively on defense. That the Panthers were going to play fast and if mistakes were going to be made, they were going to be made going 100 miles per hour. So far, I’d call that mission accomplished. Starting from the Saints first drive of the game, the differences in approach were obvious and so were the dividends they paid. Instead of lining up 7 yards off the line of srimmage, the defensive backs stood right across from their receivers and challenged them every step of the way. Instead of the free slant being available that became the signature of Ejiro Evero’s defense, Marco Wilson was in position to contest the route and popped the ball in the air and into the waiting arms of Devin Lloyd. Shough’s pass is tipped and picked by Devin Lloyd! CARvsNO on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/qk2YTor0QA — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 It’s more than just how the secondary is playing, as the lineman seem to have much less to think about and are given the green light to rush the passer without having to be as mindful of their gaps. I would even hypothesize that their aggressiveness to attack immediately off the snap instead of reading and reacting to the offense is a likely cause of the offsides, encroachment, and neutral zone infraction penalties that have popped up the last two games. Reel in the pre-snap penalties while maintaining the level of pressure on the opposing offense and we might be on to something. Personnel changes and deployment With the adjustments to scheme and philosophy there are also a few notable changes in personnel. Rookie safety Zakee Wheatley has seemingly usurped Nick Scott as the starting safety after playing 100% of the defensive snaps. With that, Scott still sees plenty of action after moving over to being more the team’s nickel defender. Chau Smith-Wade, who was once penciled in as the Panthers starting nickel has taken over as the full-time starter at one of the outside corner spots. Notably, Wheatley’s rookie classmate saw a minor tick up in snaps on Sunday with 15 compared to 13 versus the Denver Broncos. It may not seem like many, but 15 was the third most amongst defensive lineman behind Derrick Brown and Tershawn Wharton. Hunter should see more than 15 snaps a game going forward if he remains the teams 3rd defensive lineman especially if the sub-package featuring Patrick Jones lining up against an offensive guard is used any less going forward. This package got plenty of use and led to many of the Tyler Shough’s many struggles against the pressure, but I don’t expect it to be a constant in each game. Production It’s not complicated, the players that are supposed to be good have to play like it. On Sunday, many of the players the Panthers rely upon rose to the occasion. Two players in particular looked like the two best on the field on either team. That was Chuba Hubbard and Jaelen Phillips. Hubbard channeled 2019 Christian McCaffrey on Sunday by playing 85% of snaps, piling up 170 yards on 32 touches with 2 scores. The comparison to McCaffrey goes beyond the statistics, as Hubbard’s moves on the field had me double checking what year it was. I’m not kidding, when was the last time you saw a Panthers running back make a man miss in the open field like this and take it another 30 yards up field? While Hubbard willed the team to victory on offense, Phillips was determined to make the Saints right tackle want to retire. Phillip’s was dominant racking up one sack that counted, and another that should have counted if not for a questionable decision by the officials to call a horse caller for a tackle that occurred within the pocket. Alas, we’ll just have to settle for a few tackles for a loss and 8 pressures going by NFL’s NextGenStats and Sumer Sports. Not bad. Week 10 SumerStar: Jaelan Phillips The Panthers edge rusher leads the league in pressures this week with 8 pic.twitter.com/fcn6OFQemv — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) November 16, 2026 Shout outs to Derrick Brown who finally notched his first sack of the season and Monroe Freeling, the Panthers first round pick this year and frequent starter at right tackle, who played his best games a pro. Only allowing 1 pressure and having a few dominant reps in the running game is what you want to see from a first year player looking to earn their stripes. Now, time will have to tell how ‘real’ the Panthers are going forward. To be blunt, the Saints are not a good team and the Panthers looked at moments like they should have won by 2 or even 3 scores despite very nearly losing. Against a better opponent, the Panthers will not have the same margin for error. Let’s see how they hold up next week when they take on the Baltimore Ravens. Until then, keep pounding.

title: Chicago Bears 1-on-1: Can Theo Benedet neutralize the Saints’ Chase Young?
summary: On paper, the New Orleans Saints might be the worst team the Chicago Bears have faced since Week 4 against the New York Jets. The Saints rank 15th in the league in scoring offense at 22.4 points per game. They are 25th in the league in scoring defense at 26.2 ppg allowed. They are an […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 15: Chase Young #99 of the New Orleans Saints pumps up the crowd during the second half of a game against the Carolina Panthers at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On paper, the New Orleans Saints might be the worst team the Chicago Bears have faced since Week 4 against the New York Jets. The Saints rank 15th in the league in scoring offense at 22.4 points per game. They are 25th in the league in scoring defense at 26.2 ppg allowed. They are an average to below-average team, but they might yet surprise the Bears. The Saints still have a lot to play for, despite their 3-6 record. They remain only one game back in the paltry NFC South, and remain in the upswing of a franchise rebuild eager to get a taste of the postseason. Their star player right now is WR Chris Olave, who is 8th in the NFL with 764 receiving yards. He has turned into a true WR1 in his age 26 season. If after Chris Olave you are struggling to name many Saints players, that’s understandable. Their roster is young and lacking in top-end talent. But there is something lurking beneath the surface that the Bears need to take very seriously. New Orleans has two of the top four sack leaders in the NFL right now, with DE Carl Granderson boasting 8.5 sacks and his foil Chase Young sporting 8 sacks. 16.5 sacks between two players 9 games into a season is not a coincidence. While Granderson may have the higher count presently, he typically lines up on the right side and will face Darnell Wright, who is… really freaking good. It’s no given, but I think that Wright should be able to hold his own. On the other side, though, is the far more interesting matchup. Chase Young, the revived 2nd overall pick in the 2020 draft, has found a new home in New Orleans and has really turned into one of the premier pass-rushers in the league. He gets the opportunity to line up on the Bears left side, which will likely be manned by Theo Benedet. Benedet is hitting a stride himself and holds the 3rd best OT pass blocking win rate in the league entering Week 11 at 92%. He has earned the right to start at LT until Ozzy Trapilo can prove himself to be healthy enough to play like he did in 2025. Still, Chase Young’s physicality is elite. Just look at what he did against highly touted rookie Spencer Fano. Chase Young vs Spencer Fano. The former 2nd overall pick (2020) gave the Browns rookie LT SERIOUS problems 👀😳 pic.twitter.com/FwjyMAhtj3 — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) November 9, 2026 Benedet, as we know, was not a high-end draft pick. And while he has improved drastically in his third season with the Bears, he will have his hands full going up against Young. If the Bears are to win on Sunday, devising a plan to help Benedet will be crucial. It will also be important for Theo to step up and win 1-on-1s when his number is called.

It was great for the Bears to pause and have a chance to get healthy, but now is where the stakes are really going to go up. The schedule is full of playoff-hopeful teams, and that includes four more games against the NFC North gauntlet. Much is being made of Chicago’s Super Bowl chances after their 7-2 start. Now they actually have to go out and prove it. Let’s see where the Bears rank heading into their final eight games. WCG – Aaron Leming 4. Chicago Bears (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Survive a brutal schedule down the stretch and hope that Jeffery Simmons continues to be a difference-maker Once dubbed a prime regression candidate heading into the regular season, the Bears have survived without Caleb Williams for three games and somehow continue to play much better defense than the numbers suggest. Williams’ Year 3 jump has been notable, even with a four-interception game in Week 9. The talent on offense is evident, and their ceiling feels safe with Ben Johnson calling plays. How far they go this season will come down to the defense, especially the secondary. We’ll see if not making another move at the deadline comes back to bite them. The Athletic – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall 6. Chicago Bears (7-2) Last week: 6 Sunday: Bye Breakout player: Luther Burden Ben Johnson was bullish about his second-year wide receiver in the preseason, and we’re seeing why. Burden is 16th in the league with 644 receiving yards, and 385 of those came in his last four games. From weeks 6 through 9, he had more receiving yards than all but five players in the league, and he got 23.5 percent of the Bears’ passing targets. That last number may go up as the season progresses. Pro Football Talk – Mike Florio Bears (No. 5; 7-2): They can’t afford to overlook the Saints, four days before a showdown with the Lions. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 5. Chicago Bears (7-2, LW: 4) The Bears didn’t do anything wrong on their bye week. They didn’t “move down.” The Bengals just moved up after one of the most impressive games of the season. Lingering for the Bears is their home defeat to the Vikings in Week 2. They lost 9-3, and based on how the Vikings looked with Kirk Cousins in Week 10, that could be a problem. The Bears play at Minnesota in Week 18 and that’s looking like an early candidate to be flexed to the final Sunday night slot. Chicago is 0-2 in the division (Minnesota is 3-1) and that could also be bad for tiebreakers. The Lions suffered a massive injury to Aidan Hutchinson on Sunday and the Packers lost ground with a bad loss, so the NFC North could evolve into a two-team race. And the Bears might need to win in Minneapolis in Week 18 to take the division. NFL.com – Nick Shook 6. Chicago Bears (4) Having spent last week on a bye, the Bears didn’t do anything wrong — they just got caught up in a Power Rankings shakeup, with a couple of impressive teams leap-frogging them. Last time out, Chicago earned a narrow win over Tampa Bay that exposed some weaknesses but also felt like an anomaly in the larger picture. I still have plenty of confidence in this team, but it has to navigate the incredibly competitive NFC North to fulfill its potential. The Bears need to come out of the break on the right foot, facing a three-week stretch that includes dates with Detroit and Jacksonville. USAToday – Nate Davis 3. Chicago Bears (3): An offense that runs the ball more than any other in the league is about to get RB Kyle Monangai back − which is akin to making a trade deadline acquisition for free. ESPN NFL Nation – Courtney Cronin 4. Chicago Bears (7-2) Week 10 result: Bye Week 10 ranking: 4 Non-QB MVP at midseason: RB D’Andre Swift The Bears have maintained a top-five rushing offense (142 yards per game) despite a constant wave of injuries in the backfield. A big reason for that is the load Swift has carried in Kyle Monangai’s five-game absence (toe/thumb). Swift has logged the third-most offensive snaps of any Bears skill player (63%), including 22 rushes against the Patriots and 27 at Seattle a week later. He ran in three second-half TDs against the Seahawks, has already reached a career high of 10 TDs and is five away from setting the franchise’s single-season record. Despite dealing with injuries of his own, Swift has not missed a game. — Courtney Cronin CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 4. Chicago Bears (4) They entered their bye as one of the league’s hottest teams. Does it stay that way? There is nothing to think it won’t. What do you think of this week’s rankings? The idle week didn’t hurt them much, if at all.

title: Bears have a tough path to the playoffs, but are focused on 1-0
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. The Chicago Bears may have dropped from the second seed to sixth in the conference standings during their bye, but they are still firmly in the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after a touchdown against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first quarter at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. The Chicago Bears may have dropped from the second seed to sixth in the conference standings during their bye, but they are still firmly in the NFC postseason mix at 7-2. The NFC North is the NFL’s toughest division, and the Bears (on paper) have the toughest remaining schedule, but Caleb Williams and the Bears aren’t looking ahead, and they’re 100% focused on the New Orleans Saints this Sunday. When asked how they stay in the moment and not get caught up in the division race and playoff positioning, Williams said , “The point of it is that we have to do our part, and our part is going 1-0 each week. I think that’s what it comes down to. You don’t focus on eight games from now because we haven’t played those eight games. You don’t focus on next week or the week after and who we got and prime times or the non-prime times.” ”You focus on being prepared for that moment of when the the ball gets snapped the first time, whistle gets blown, and we focus on being 1-0 that week. And then when the next one comes up, we’ll focus on being 1-0 that week. And if you go 1-0 each week and you focus on that each week, you’ll turn out to kind of be where you want to be at the end of it.” Head coach Ben Johnson also met the media today, and it’s not hard to figure out where Caleb’s 1-0 mindset comes from. When asked about his big-picture take on the NFC North, Johnson said , “It really doesn’t matter right now. Once again, it’s all about winning this week. So, we’ll worry about everything else when it’s time. It’s not time for that. There’s still eight games to be played, and this is the most important one because it’s the next one.” The Bears host the Saints on Sunday at Noon. title: Chicago Bears Stock Watch: Burden, Booker up, Johnson, Santos down
summary: It’s over the halfway mark of the season for the Chicago Bears. Since the 17-game season came in, there is no longer a nice and neat halfway point to the schedule. But having a bye week after nine games is a good-enough mark to take stock over players that have risen and fallen over the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks during the first quarter of the game at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s over the halfway mark of the season for the Chicago Bears. Since the 17-game season came in, there is no longer a nice and neat halfway point to the schedule. But having a bye week after nine games is a good-enough mark to take stock over players that have risen and fallen over the first nine games of the season. I am sticking to my usual three in each category, so it isn’t going to be comprehensive. There are many players worthy of inclusion on the up list. I’ll toss in some honorable memtions for good measure, too. Stock up Luther Burden, WR – Ben Johnson told us to buy stock in Burden way back in May. Now I was already holding some from his days at Missouri and more following his rookie season in Chicago. But the buy has paid off. Burden leads the team in receptions, yards and touchdowns. He’s on pace for a 1,200 yard season. He’s been great at gaining YAC and making catches at all levels. I am excited to see what he’s capable of in the stretch run of the season. Austin Booker, DE – Expectations have perhaps been unfairly high for Booker. He flashed enough that his injury-shortened second season and lack of moves on the DL put pressure on him by fans to step up. And he has. While still not consistent, I think he’s been a great complement to the line alongside Jeffery Simmons and Montez Sweat. He has a new-career high in sacks with 5 this year and he is solidly the DE3 following Dayo Odeyingbo’s injury. Malik Muhammad, CB – Coming into the season, the expectations for the offense and the roles of those players were straightforward. The defense was the side with all the questions. In some ways, the worst has been the case (see the stock down), but Muhammad has actually been Chicago’s most consistent corner. He’s been a notable absence since his injury. Honorable mentions: Dillon Thieneman, Devin Bush Jr., Kalif Raymond and Daniel Hardy Stock down Jaylon Johnson, CB – Any hopes of a return to form from before his core injury in 2024 are long gone. Johnson had a rough start to the season. His interception touchdown against the Bucs was a high-point, but I think we all know that those moments will be fewer and farther between. Hopefully, he can build on it and use his experience to win matchups in the second half of the season. Tyson Bagent, QB – Pressed into action following Caleb Williams’ hamstring injury, Bagent unfortunately didn’t do much to inspire confidence about him being a potential NFL starter. He’s still a decent backup QB but any hopes of a trade with meaningful draft capital disappeared following his interception-filled games against the Jets and Packers. Cairo Santos, K – He’s coming off a game-winning field goal, so I understand there might be some frustration with his appearance here. But he currently has the lowest FG percentage of his Bears career at 78.9 percent. Sure, the one block got his long snapper back on the practice squad, but he missed one from 40-49. If you’re not a big-leg kicker, you have to make ‘em all from inside 50 yards. Plus, landing-zone penalties are unforced errors. Honorable mentions: Garrett Bradbury, T.J. Edwards, Tyrique Stevenson Who do you think has been up and who has been down over the first nine games?

title: Chicago Bears will re-establish their running game post-bye
summary: As the Chicago Bears embrace a deep playoff run, Head Coach Ben Johnson understands the importance of getting the run game back on track to its dominant self. The return of Kyle Monangai will be an obvious boost, but Coach Johnson indicated some schematic changes will be implemented coming out of the BYE week. Speaking […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after making a play during the first quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Chicago Bears embrace a deep playoff run, Head Coach Ben Johnson understands the importance of getting the run game back on track to its dominant self. The return of Kyle Monangai will be an obvious boost, but Coach Johnson indicated some schematic changes will be implemented coming out of the BYE week. Speaking with Chicago Bears media Senior Writer Larry Mayer , Coach had this to say. “We’re going to take a look at what we’re doing well right now, what we’re most consistent at,” Johnson said. “Schematically, we’re a little bit different in terms of where we were this year compared to last year. [But] there are some things coming out of last year’s bye week that we’re able to lean into, and I’m hoping that we’re going to be able to find some nuggets like that of areas that we really can make more consistent. “Over the course of nine games, there’s only been three where we’re averaging four yards a carry, which simply is just not good enough right now. Those guys know that. Particularly as the weather continues to turn into ‘Bear weather,’ we’re going to need to lean on that run game more. It’s going to need to come through for us.” Context is always important, like the fact that Chicago has played two of the top 5 rushing defenses in the league in yards per game allowed in the last two weeks, but Coach is on to something. Ever since Monangai went down, the Bears’ rushing output has decreased from 196.3 yards per game to just under 100 per game. While D’Andre Swift has done an admirable job shouldering the load in those games – all but 1 win – he clearly needs his running mate back, and it would appear there is more to unlock from a schematic standpoint similar to last season. A year ago, Chicago’s adjustments during the BYE week led to them amassing more than 150 yards rushing on five separate occasions to finish the season, when they hadn’t eclipsed 140 in any game prior to the BYE. When you combine a mastermind play-caller with the arguably best RB2 in the league, good things are bound to happen. Add in some chilly Chicago weather, and we very well may once again get to see a powerful run game propel the Bears into the postseason. The question then becomes: Can they continue that momentum all the way to the Super Bowl this time? Time will tell. But I, for one, am excited to see even more complementary football moving forward. In your opinion, is Coach Johnson’s offensive genius OR Kyle Monangai’s return more critical to the run game moving forward?
author: Bryan Orenchuk

title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL, Week 10: The Kings in the North
summary: 1. Take a bow, Joe Burrow. Show me a guy playing the quarterback position better than that guy right now. Sure, it’s nice to be able to throw to Ja’Marr Chase (11 catches for 231 yards), who is right there with Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Justin Jefferson as the very best receivers in football, and Tee […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - NOVEMBER 15: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals celebrates after a touchdown during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Paycor Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images 1. Take a bow, Joe Burrow. Show me a guy playing the quarterback position better than that guy right now. Sure, it’s nice to be able to throw to Ja’Marr Chase (11 catches for 231 yards), who is right there with Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Justin Jefferson as the very best receivers in football, and Tee Higgins. But if you’re watching these games, you know what you’re seeing: a quarterback operating at a level few have ever reached. The Bengals’ passing offense was so unstoppable that Cincinnati didn’t even have to run the ball. When Burrow can complete 35 of 44 attempts for 409 yards and four touchdowns, why would you? If you’re asking me to pick an MVP through the halfway point of the season, Burrow’s mine. 2. This is the second straight year the NFC North is inarguably the best division in football. What a time to be alive. Every team in the division has at least six wins so far, with three of those teams (Minnesota, Detroit, and Chicago) sitting at 7-2. And every time they play one another, they’re out there throwing absolute haymakers. Even as a Bears homer, it’s hard to definitively say who the best team in this division is because they won’t stop clobbering the rest of the league, and you have no idea what you’re going to get when they play one another. There is a legitimate chance that every team in the NFC North finishes with a winning record, but someone misses the playoffs again. How cruel is that? (As long as it’s not the Bears…) 3. I don’t agree with Dan Orlovsky on much, but I found myself reluctantly nodding to his take about Aidan Hutchinson after the latter suffered a season-ending knee injury celebrating a sack on Drake Maye. Being amped about getting a sack is great and well-earned. Dance. Pump the fist. Do whatever you want. But keep your feet on the ground when you’re doing it. We’ve seen too many LaMarr Houston situations to have our pass-rushers keep going down like this. That’s now Hutchinson’s second major knee injury in three seasons, and it’s going to hurt a Lions team that keeps outperforming expectations. 4. The Chargers’ unlikely quest to go 0-17 is finally over. And they needed all the Ravens’ help to get it done, too. I love me some Zay Flowers, but man…it’s okay to go down or run out of bounds sometimes. These devastating fumbles have to stop. Then again, not unlike the Patriots now that they’ve likely lost Drake Maye for the season, Baltimore is already cooked without Lamar Jackson. Great tank loss for the Ravens, especially considering Jacoby Brissett, who just got there a few hours ago, played pretty well all things considered. 5. You know what it means that Dak Prescott (343 yards, 5 TDs) had a QBR of 85.2 on Sunday against the San Francisco 49ers, according to ESPN? It means that he played at basically an All-Pro level. That, even though Brock Purdy (389 yards, 3 TDs) also balled out, there’s no reason that the Cowboys should lose a game in which Prescott played that well. But they did. Because the Cowboys are a joke (outside of Prescott). Because their lame-duck coach never deserved to be there in the first place, and their geriatric owner is more concerned with upholding the good ol’ boys club than winning football games. Because Dallas decided not to cover Christian McCaffrey, the literal best skill player on the team, twice and let Deebo Samuel score on the most Pop Warner-esque play of all time. Free Dak. 6. Who would’ve thought that the moment Patrick Mahomes gets a slot receiver worth a damn, he immediately goes off for five touchdown passes? Seriously, keep an eye on that Josh Downs move to Kansas City as the season goes on. For him to net 53 yards and a score off rip says a lot for his talent and what the Chiefs’ receiving pecking order looks like. While Rashee Rice is clearly the top dog, KC has been searching a while for that slot receiver who can make explosive plays and make Mahomes’ life easier. While no one is quite the cheat code Tyreek Hill was, Downs is plenty good enough. Can’t wait to see how that partnership grows as the year progresses. Lord knows the Colts weren’t worth Downs’ time. 7. It might just be because they play in Jacksonville, and too many people are used to them being awful. But boy, are those Jaguars popping right now. If Joe Burrow is the MVP of the league right now, Trevor Lawrence (2,284 yards, 21 TDs, 5 INTs on the season; 352 yards, 3 TDs on Sunday) is on the short list of runners-up. The funny part: as good as they are on offense right now (fourth in points scored), they’re just as scary on defense (second-fewest points allowed). Something tells me this isn’t the year the Jags win it all. But win a playoff game? I can see it. 8. I don’t care what Donte Whitner says: I thought Jameis Winston having fun with his dummy calls was hilarious. At a certain point, when the defense isn’t jumping and the offense clearly isn’t interested in running a play, you know what the score is. If they didn’t jump on the first few honest attempts to draw them offside, they’re not going to jump with three seconds left on the play clock. In the end, it’s a game. Have fun. It’s not his fault the Washington Commanders gave up that game-losing touchdown and JJ McCarthy threw that pick. Be mad at them. 9. Since I mentioned him earlier, I just want to say it once more: JSN is one of the best receivers I’ve ever seen. And I told a lot of people he would be coming out of college, but people just couldn’t let go of his 40 time. Does he look slow out there while he’s ripping off long touchdowns and putting up 79 catches for 1,207 yards through 10 games? Anyone want to tell me why they thought Quentin Johnston was going to have a better career just because he was 6-4 and could run fast in a straight line? And again, he’s doing this with Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, doesn’t matter. Whether he breaks the single-season record for receiving yards or not, he’s the best of his generation. And again, when he’s putting his resume up against those LSU monstrosities Jefferson and Chase, that’s saying a lot . 10. You know what? Let’s make that the question of the week, and it’s actually a great one because all of them have such unique skill sets. Which Big 3 receiver would you take: JSN, Jefferson, or Chase? Personally, I’m going JSN<Chase<Jefferson, with the margins so narrow you have to look into an electron microscope to see the gaps. How about you?

title: Week 11 NFL Power Rankings: Each Team’s Second-Half Outlook
summary: Although it might be hard to believe, we’ve not only crossed the halfway point of the 2026 NFL regular season, but the trade deadline has come and gone, too. While the NFC playoff picture is muddied with nine very good teams fighting for seven playoff spots, the AFC is a little easier to decipher. With […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 15: DJ Moore #2 of the Buffalo Bills catches a touchdown against Malachi Moore #27 of the New York Jets in the third quarter of a game at MetLife Stadium on November 15, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images Although it might be hard to believe, we’ve not only crossed the halfway point of the 2026 NFL regular season, but the trade deadline has come and gone, too. While the NFC playoff picture is muddied with nine very good teams fighting for seven playoff spots, the AFC is a little easier to decipher. With the stretch run upon us, it’s time to take a deeper dive into every team’s second-half outlook. While many are still competing for a playoff spot, others will need to find meaning amid lost seasons. We’ll dive into all of that and more in our Week 11 installment of WCG NFL Power Rankings. 1. San Francisco 49ers (8-1) Second-Half Outlook: Get healthy and continue their push for the No. 1 seed in the NFC The first nine games of the season have been nothing short of impressive for the 49ers. Looking back to the preseason, nobody had the 49ers running away with a loaded NFC West, especially with the defending Super Bowl Champions and the overwhelming 2026 Super Bowl favorites. Instead, Kyle Shanahan has taken one of the league’s oldest rosters and survived multiple impact injuries. We’ll see if they can keep the pace up over the back half of the year, but this is one of the more well-rounded rosters in the league this season. 2. Buffalo Bills (8-1) Second-Half Outlook: Hope that the defense can round into form and support one of the league’s elite offenses The addition of Amani Hooker should be a big one for this Buffalo defense, but it’s fair to wonder if one player will be enough to turn the tide for a struggling defense. Some might point to their Week 8 and 9 performances as hope, and while that might be the case, the opponents need to be noted. The good news is that this is an experienced roster with an MVP-caliber quarterback. We’ll see if they finally have enough to get them over the hump in the AFC. Like last year, it’s wide open and theirs for the taking. 3. Jacksonville Jaguars (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Ride a favorable schedule and find a way to earn the No. 1 seed down the stretch The Bills might have better odds to win the Super Bowl, but the Jaguars have a strong argument for being the more well-rounded team. Simply put, Jacksonville has been dominant for the majority of the season, and the additions of Jordan Davis and Devin Godchaux should help stabilize the middle of their defense. If quarterback Trevor Lawrence can continue his ascension, this is going to be the toughest out for anybody in the AFC. 4. Chicago Bears (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Survive a brutal schedule down the stretch and hope that Jeffery Simmons continues to be a difference-maker Once dubbed a prime regression candidate heading into the regular season, the Bears have survived without Caleb Williams for three games and somehow continue to play much better defense than the numbers suggest. Williams’ Year 3 jump has been notable, even with a four-interception game in Week 9. The talent on offense is evident, and their ceiling feels safe with Ben Johnson calling plays. How far they go this season will come down to the defense, especially the secondary. We’ll see if not making another move at the deadline comes back to bite them. 5. Cincinnati Bengals (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Continue to build continuity on defense and hope that they’ll be good enough to get them over the hump down the stretch and into January When quarterback Joe Burrow is healthy, this offense is hard to stop. Their running game has been spotty at best, but with Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins on the field, it really hasn’t mattered. Their defense is much improved from previous seasons, but there are still some holes that could expose them against better teams. The AFC North appears to be coming down to the Bengals and Steelers, and at full strength, I’d take Cincinnati without much thought. Similar to the Bills, their defense will dictate how far they can go this season. So far, so good. 6. Kansas City Chiefs (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Hope that Patrick Mahomes is healthy enough to enjoy his new offensive weapon and push the Broncos for the AFC West title Despite their 5-0 start to the season, I’m still not ready to say the Chiefs are all the way “back”. They’ve continued to ignore the wide receiver position, and while the addition of Josh Downs is a step in the right direction, there’s still a lot to be desired on the offensive side of the ball when it comes to personnel. Keeping Mahomes healthy will be key, and their Week 9 scare could have been season-altering. They aren’t out of the race in the AFC West, but the offensive production is going to need to jump in the second half for them to win the division. 7. Detroit Lions (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Rely on a weak schedule down the stretch and hope that the defense can continue to play at the same level In many ways, the start of this season has been eerily similar to how they looked last season. So far, the biggest difference is that they are winning those close games that they couldn’t pull off last season. The offense has looked great under Drew Petzing, but their season will come down to how much their defense can sustain over the final eight games. Following a rough start, they’ve been playing much better as of late, but there are still plenty of questions on that side of the ball. In a loaded NFC North, they must take advantage of their favorable schedule. Missing Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson will hurt, especially over time. 8. Minnesota Vikings (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Hope that the presence of Kirk Cousins is enough to support an elite defense Defensively, there isn’t a better unit in the league. Frankly, with as poor as their offense has played to this point, Brian Flores’ group is the only thing separating them from a losing record. With that in mind, the addition of Cousins comes at a great time. Not only are they in the midst of their toughest stretch of the season, but the veteran quarterback knows the offense and should be able to hit the ground running. Even if he’s still the fourth-best quarterback in his own division, the ceiling for the offense is considerably higher than it was just a week ago. We saw that on Sunday in Green Bay. Now, we’ll see if that’s good enough to separate themselves in a loaded NFC North. 9. Denver Broncos (7-2) Second-Half Outlook: Hope that Bo Nix can take his play up a notch (or two) to make them legitimate Super Bowl contenders in January Very rarely does a team’s fortune in one-score games carry over (good or bad) from season to season the way that the Broncos have. Even with Nix struggling for the majority of the season, they are a seven-win team in full control of their destiny. The defense remains elite, and if Nix can figure out a way to start challenging downfield more, there’s no reason they can’t find their way back to the AFC Championship game again this season. Even with the Daiyan Henley deal falling through, there’s little reason to doubt this defense. 10. Los Angeles Rams (6-4) Second-Half Outlook: Get healthy on both sides of the ball and hope that their slow start doesn’t keep them out of the playoffs come January Despite coming into the season as the overwhelming Super Bowl favorites, the Rams haven’t been healthy enough to reach their ceiling. While there’s still time for that to happen, Puka Nacua’s trip to Injured Reserve is a tough blow to absorb, especially with Davante Adams still a few weeks away from returning. The NFC is loaded, and even for as talented as Los Angeles is, they face an uphill battle to make the playoffs. We’ll see if quarterback Matthew Stafford can elevate his play without his two best receivers. Their season might depend on it. 11. Seattle Seahawks (6-4) Second-Half…
