title: Steelers Week 11 power rankings roundup: Pittsburgh slides after loss to Bengals
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers were embarrassed by the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on Sunday night. It was by far the Steelers’ worst showing of the season, as their defense was shredded for 409 yards through the air while posting 222 total yards themselves. The Bengals gained sole possession of first place in the AFC North, […]
full_text: (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers were embarrassed by the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on Sunday night. It was by far the Steelers’ worst showing of the season, as their defense was shredded for 409 yards through the air while posting 222 total yards themselves. The Bengals gained sole possession of first place in the AFC North, putting the Steelers in a tough spot to repeat as AFC North champions. As always, let’s take a look around the internet to see where the Steelers fall on this week’s power rankings roundup. FOX Sports: No.15 (No. 12 Last Week) “In the words of former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin, speaking on the Sunday Night Football postgame show, “they got smashed” by the Bengals. They really did. They were smashed into a 31-3 hole in the third quarter before Aaron Rodgers and the offense showed a pulse. In fact, they had 23 total yards through three quarters, including minus-17 in the third quarter alone. And their defense wasn’t any better. It was a good, old-fashioned butt-kicking. And it proved that the Bengals, not the Steelers, are far and away the power team in the AFC North this year.” – Ralph Vacchiano The Athletic: No.13 (Last Week No.13) “The fifth-year running back was disappointing Sunday night, but so were all of the other Steelers. For the season, Warren has been great. He has 126 carries for 719 yards and leads all running backs with 5.7 yards per carry. He’s second in the league in yards per carry after contact (4.04).” – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall CBS Sports: No.10 (Last Week No. 9) “The offense couldn’t keep up with the Bengals as the defense was shredded by Joe Burrow. That was not a good look Sunday night.” – Pete Prisco Pro Football Talk: No.11 (Last Week No. 7) “They’re not ready to compete with the best teams in the conference.” – Mike Florio NFL.com: No.13 (Last Week No.12) “I expected more from the Steelers on Sunday night . I knew the offense had its issues, but I did not expect them to allow the Bengals to cruise right through their defense, especially after Pittsburgh had the bye week to prepare for this massive AFC North showdown. It may have just been a bad day at the office, but I tend to believe it might also be a reminder of this team’s flaws and overall limitations.” – Nick Shook Yahoo! Sports: No.13 (Last Week No.13) “Was Sunday’s outing just a bad night against a hot Bengals team or a bad sign for the Steelers going forward? It’s OK to excuse it as a one-off. Before the 38-18 blowout loss, the Steelers were 6-2 and showing improvement. It’s also OK to worry that Pittsburgh was exposed, though Aaron Rodgers didn’t think so when asked if the loss changes the season’s trajectory.” “That’s very dramatic,” Rodgers said, via the team’s site . “I’ve been a part of this league for a long time. There’s big wins, there’s tough losses, so we’ll deal with this properly.” “One thing that is an issue for the Steelers is their receiver room. DK Metcalf continued to have minimal impact, as he was held without a catch before garbage time in the fourth quarter. Germie Bernard was blanked and has just 57 yards in Pittsburgh’s last three games. No other healthy receiver on the roster has more than 39 yards this season. Roman Wilson and Michael Pittman Jr. could both return in the next couple weeks, and that is badly needed.” – Frank Schwab USA Today: No.13 (Last Week No.13) Another chapter in this franchise’s storied history, the Steelers now with the distinction of being the first team coming off a bye week to lose to an opponent coming back from a game in Europe. – Nate Davis ESPN: No.13 (Last Week No. 13) “Even after a quiet night in the Steelers’ blowout loss to the Bengals, Warren is still far and away the Steelers’ MVP. He ranks sixth among all players in yards from scrimmage (1,039) this season and has a league-best 5.7 yards per carry. Warren also ranks fifth in rushing yards after contact (364). Given Pittsburgh’s inconsistent and ineffective passing game, Warren is the Steelers’ most reliable option to move the ball.” – Brooke Pryor As humiliating as the loss was for the Steelers, it seems as though the national media is giving the Steelers some leeway. Of the eight publications we examined today, only two of them moved the Steelers multiple spots down in their rankings. Half of them kept the Steelers in the same spot. The Steelers are viewed as a good team that can’t quite play with the top-of-the-line teams in the NFL, and that seems like a pretty spot-on evaluation at this point in the season. full_text: (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers were taken to the woodshed on Sunday night by the division-leading Cincinnati Bengals. Now, one win isn’t the end of the world, but it was a measuring-stick game and feels disappointing to put forth that effort on national television. The defense couldn’t get stops, and yes, the Bengals and Joe Burrow are on a tear, but the effort was poor. With over 400 passing yards allowed, Pittsburgh’s defense was on the ropes all night. The two split their meetings, and Pittsburgh has to pick up the pieces with the remaining schedule of Philadelphia, Denver, Houston, Jacksonville, and Baltimore. A 3-2 record has to be the goal at the very least. But you also can’t rule out the 6-4 Browns, whose favorable schedule could lead to a surprise division win. Here is Tuesday’s Three Rivers Report. summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers may finally be getting one of their to receivers back in the lineup in Week 11. full_text: (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers may finally be getting one of their to receivers back in the lineup in Week 11. Mark Kaboly of the Pat McAfee Show reported on Tuesday morning that wide receiver Roman Wilson is trending toward coming off injured reserve and playing in Week 11 as the team travels to Philadelphia to take on the Eagles. It's trending toward Steelers WR Roman Wilson coming off the IR this week and playing Sunday against the Eagles. pic.twitter.com/rC62jorV2o — Mark Kaboly (@MarkKaboly) November 17, 2026 Yesterday in his weekly press conference, Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy said he was “hopeful” to have both Wilson and Michael Pittman Jr. back this week to help bolster the receiver room. At least one of them is now likely to return this week. Wilson has been on injured reserve since Week 5 after suffering a finger injury against the Indianapolis Colts. The 84th pick in the 2024 NFL Draft has already posted a career high in receiving yards this season with 188 in five games played. Wilson had emerged as a downfield threat for Rodgers and one of the Steelers’ best man coverage beaters before his injury. Wilson’s return should provide a boost to the Steelers’ passing game that has been lackluster for several weeks now. The Steelers have yet to open the 21-day practice window for the receiver, which they would then have to activate him for him to be eligible to play this Sunday. With the team not practicing on Tuesdays, Wednesday should give us a clearer view of the team’s plans for the receiver this weekend. Let us know what you think in the comments . full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers are hosting former Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Nazeeh Johnson for a workout on Tuesday, per Jordan Schultz . Johnson was drafted in the seventh round of the 2022 NFL Draft by the Chiefs out of Marshall. He appeared in 11 games as a rookie, but missed all of 2023 with an injury and was placed on IR in July. He was part of the Chiefs’ 2024 Super Bowl-winning team, appearing in 16 games and registering 56 tackles and three pass breakups. He found himself on IR again ahead of the 2025 season and appeared in just two games. He signed with the Tennessee Titans this past offseason, but was suspended for the first six games of the year due to violating the NFL’s policy against PEDs, and he was waived in early September. The Steelers have an obvious need at cornerback after Ja’Marr Chase torched their secondary for 231 receiving yards. Should the Steelers add Johnson to the roster, it could be the beginning of the end for Asante Samuel Jr, who was credited with giving up five receptions for 135 yards against Cincinnati, per Next Gen Stats . title: Why Seahawks vs. 49ers wasn’t flexed to ‘Sunday Night Football’ over Raiders vs. Browns
summary: The NFL made the merciful decision to pull the New England Patriots at Los Angeles Chargers from the Week 12 Sunday Night Football lineup on Tuesday, marking the first primetime “flex” of the 2026 season. With slim pickings on Thanksgiving weekend, the replacement game is the 4-6 Las Vegas Raiders at the 6-4 Cleveland Browns. […]
full_text: The NFL made the merciful decision to pull the New England Patriots at Los Angeles Chargers from the Week 12 Sunday Night Football lineup on Tuesday, marking the first primetime “flex” of the 2026 season . With slim pickings on Thanksgiving weekend, the replacement game is the 4-6 Las Vegas Raiders at the 6-4 Cleveland Browns. Mind you, the Seattle Seahawks play the San Francisco 49ers in a potentially seismic rematch on the same day. So why was Seahawks-49ers shunned from primetime? It’s the media rights rulebook more than not being interested in a superior game. FOX likely “protected” Seahawks vs. 49ers In order to satisfy all rights holders, FOX and CBS recently had expanded abilities to protect marquee matchups from being poached and put on NBC, ESPN, or Prime Video for flex scheduling purposes. During the flex windows from Weeks 5-17, FOX and CBS are allowed to essentially make one game flex-proof, usually a lead 10 am or 1 pm PT game. The first Seahawks vs. 49ers game aired nationally on FOX, in part because of a flex schedule decision to move the Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers to the early window. By rule, FOX was already entitled to at least one of the two Seahawks-49ers games as a key divisional matchup, so they were essentially in good position to broadcast both the entire time. As a 1:25 pm PT kickoff, it’ll still be FOX’s feature late game, so most of the country will be watching. Emphasis on most , because… The Seahawks-49ers rematch won’t be nationally broadcast The bad news for Seahawks fans is that unlike Week 5, the Week 12 rematch will not be a standalone doubleheader. FOX will also be showing the Washington Commanders at Arizona Cardinals in a game that will likely be limited to just the DC and Phoenix primary and secondary markets, but if you’re a Seahawks fan located in the DC and Phoenix areas then I hope you have Sunday Ticket or another means to watch the game.

title: Recently released Seahawks safeties find new teams
summary: A pair of former Seattle Seahawks safeties have made their way onto practice squads elsewhere, including someone who started on late notice earlier in the season. According to Tuesday’s NFL transaction wire, A.J. Finley signed with the Pittsburgh Steelers practice squad, having been released last week by Seattle. Finley was on injured reserve last season […]
full_text: A pair of former Seattle Seahawks safeties have made their way onto practice squads elsewhere, including someone who started on late notice earlier in the season. According to Tuesday’s NFL transaction wire, A.J. Finley signed with the Pittsburgh Steelers practice squad, having been released last week by Seattle. Finley was on injured reserve last season with a torn ACL suffered in training camp, and alternated between active roster and practice squad to start this year. He started in place of the injured Julian Love in Week 3 against the Washington Commanders, played exclusively special teams in Week 4 vs. the Los Angeles Chargers, but hasn’t had any playing time since then. Meanwhile, D’Anthony Bell has joined the Minnesota Vikings practice squad after remaining a free agent after the Seahawks let him go at the end of September. Bell was part of Seattle’s PS and active roster throughout 2025 as a special teamer and reserve safety, but when he was waived late in the year, the Carolina Panthers claimed him. Seattle nevertheless gave Bell a Super Bowl ring for his efforts . Seattle has had Ty Okada and Julian Love starting in tandem since Week 5, with Okada missing a month due to a hamstring injury. Rodney Thomas II has been the main reserve safety throughout the year, with Maxen Hook as additional practice squad depth.

full_text: The Seattle Seahawks spent a weekend in Las Vegas and left as a winner. So much for “the house always wins” when you play the Las Vegas Raiders, I suppose. Klint Kubiak’s first game against Mike Macdonald started well and fizzled out hard, with rookie QB Fernando Mendoza having his “Welcome to the NFL” moment after an early 10-7 lead. Seattle rode some explosive pass plays and dominant defense to get a 21-13 win that wasn’t as close as the score indicated. Enemy Reaction is back! We gave the Arizona Cardinals a reprieve because, well, they’re the Cardinals. The Raiders? Not so much, and I haven’t done a Raiders Enemy Reaction in eight years. (21-13 SEA FINAL) Drew Lock everybody 🔥 SEAvsLV on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/D79kLHO106 — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 Post-game recap: The good and bad from Fernando Mendoza’s debut ( Warren Mitchell, Raiders Beat ) Mendoza’s arm talent is elite He didn’t beat the Seahawks downfield, but Mendoza’s release is much quicker than Cousins’ release and going forward he is going to be able to get passes into tight windows that Cousins cannot. Mendoza was not always on the same page with his receivers, but that probably had a lot to do with his lack of first-team reps. Contrary to reports, the CBS broadcast said Mendoza didn’t get many first-team reps before last week, and the majority of the first-team reps he received before last week were running plays. Now the bad… Mendoza held onto the ball too long He had a tendency to hold on to the ball too long in college and it happened a few times on Sunday, especially in the second half. In the first half, Mendoza threw the ball away under pressure. In the second half, he held on to the ball and took unnecessary sacks. The receivers played a role in some of the sacks (they couldn’t create separation), but Mendoza still has to avoid negative plays when no one is open. Post-game video: Grading Fernando Mendoza’s debut and ripping the Raiders defense ( JT The Brick ) Enemy Preaction: San Francisco 49ers (sure, and the Dallas Cowboys too!) Don't leave CMC in the open field 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/hGnsBSY5V5 — San Francisco 49ers (@49ers) November 16, 2026 We can have a little relaxation (but only a little) for Week 11, as the Seahawks have a bye week and even immediate playoff rivals like the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers also have Week 11 off. We’ll presumably all be big Minnesota Vikings fans when they play the San Francisco 49ers in Mexico City, because that’s the one possible path for Seattle to get back into the NFC West race. Rest up, heal up, and let’s see the Seahawks have another classic second-half surge like we saw last year, and certainly in a few of the Pete Carroll years! Thanks for reading and go ‘Hawks!

title: Drew Lock saved the Seahawks’ season, but Mike Macdonald is betting on Sam Darnold
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have been through it in the 2026 season. Defending the crown has proven to be every bit as difficult as most defending champs claim, as Seattle continues to battle through injuries, turnovers, and regression of their own as the league’s contenders ascend. Adversity and the reality of potentially missing the playoffs never […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have been through it in the 2026 season. Defending the crown has proven to be every bit as difficult as most defending champs claim, as Seattle continues to battle through injuries, turnovers, and regression of their own as the league’s contenders ascend. Adversity and the reality of potentially missing the playoffs never felt more real than after the Seahawks were whooped by the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football , to fall to 4-4. Having more losses than all of the previous season already, missing your quarterback and defensive anchor, it felt like the Seahawks were on the ropes. Facing a motivated Arizona Cardinals team and a Las Vegas Raiders team full of familiar foes and the debut of “Mendoza Mania”, Mike Macdonald had to find a way to will this version of his Seahawks to go 2-0, and get to their late bye at 6-4. Mission accomplished. An absolutely dominant 120 minutes of football by the Kylo Ren version of the Dark Side Defense held Arizona and Las Vegas to 16 total points, while the offense played good football to complement the incredible Jaxon Smith-Njigba, as they mercifully arrived at the pit stop with the team nearly running on empty. The Seahawks will not be 100% healthy after the bye, but they should have a large chunk of their reinforcements back in time for their biggest game of the year, at the San Francisco 49ers. Among those players is Sam Darnold, whom we received some positive news about on Monday during the Mike Macdonald Show on 710 ESPN . On his weekly show, Macdonald stated that the team was, “really optimistic that he’s gonna be able to get a full week’s worth, and be able to play again in San Francisco.” Barring a health setback, as he has some hurdles to get over, Macdonald confirmed that Darnold would be the starting QB. I thought this was a fascinating declaration by Coach Macdonald, as both the Seahawk and NFL worlds were preparing to have a two-week war on whether the Seahawks would give the ball back to Sam, or keep riding with the undefeated Lock. Heck, even I wrote how I didn’t think there was any way you could take the ball away from Drew if he went 2-0 before the bye. When asked by Mike Salk about the process of choosing a starting QB, considering Lock has played as well as any quarterback this season, Macdonald gave a noticeable smirk and responded by saying, “Drew’s been fantastic. He’s been phenomenal, but Sam’s our quarterback” finishing his sentence with a chuckle. Macdonald would delve deeper into the “tough road” that Darnold has faced this season, from the Patriots glute injury, to him breaking his ribs on the first drive against the Bears. I thought this was a surprising, but calculated move by Macdonald. Instead of letting this QB debate heat up and become the storyline of the season (it still could happen), Macdonald essentially killed this story before the train could even get on the tracks. Macdonald has his eyes set on both the short-term and long-term game for the team and franchise as a whole. Is there a chance that Drew Lock could Nick Foles this thing, and get the Seahawks into the playoffs and make a run? Sure, but Macdonald knows that Sam can do that as well, as he saw him do just that last year, leading to a Lombardi Trophy. Is Drew’s floor safer than Sam’s right now? Absolutely, but I don’t think anyone truly believes that the Seahawks can get back to 2025 levels, with Lock. And maybe it isn’t fair to Sam for him to be considered the make or break guy as well (this is probably more of a Kubiak vs Fleury conversation, but I digress). That being said, the Seahawks need their quarterback to be able to go mano a mano with the NFC MVP candidates in Brock Purdy, Caleb Williams, and Jared Goff. Macdonald saw Sam outduel 2025 MVP Matthew Stafford just nine months ago, and this team will need that level of play again if they wish to defend their crown. I commend Macdonald doubling down on his guy, and it has to create at least a two-week window of clear focus and confidence for Darnold. He needs to get healthy, but as things stand according to Mike, the Seahawks will be going into the lion’s den on November 29 with Sam leading the charge. Drew Lock may be the safer bet to getting back to the postseason, but Sam Darnold is their best bet at making another championship run. Mike Macdonald still believes this is a championship team, and he’s betting on Darnold being the quarterback who can get them back to that status. Drew Lock may have saved Seattle’s season, but Macdonald thinks Sam is the one who can finish it. We’ll see if he’s right.

title: The Matador and the Magic King: How the 49ers can beat the most aggressive defense football has ever seen
summary: México City is home to the world’s largest bullring. On Jan. 7, 2007, Plaza México booked a 54-year-old baker’s son, Rodolfo Rodríguez, as a favor. They called it his farewell. “El Pana” showed up in a horse-drawn carriage, a cigar in his teeth, and a pink suit of lights that had seen better decades. His […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) México City is home to the world’s largest bullring. On Jan. 7, 2007, Plaza México booked a 54-year-old baker’s son, Rodolfo Rodríguez, as a favor. They called it his farewell. “El Pana” showed up in a horse-drawn carriage, a cigar in his teeth, and a pink suit of lights that had seen better decades. His bull was named Rey Mago—the Magic King. Rey Mago did what every fighting bull does. It erupted into the ring, head low, hooves digging, bred for one thing and never once asked to be gentle. And that’s exactly why it lost. Because a matador doesn’t fight the bull; he follows three words as old as the ring itself: parar, Templar mandar . Stand still. Match the charge. Command it. Hold your ground while the horns come. Slow the charge to your rhythm with the cape. Then send it exactly where you want it to go. Every whiff drains a little more of the fury. The bull never notices. The crowd does. And most importantly, the matador does. El Pana never beat Rey Mago with the sword. He beat it with the cape. By nightfall, México City wasn’t calling it a farewell. They called it his Resurrection Sunday. Sunday night, the 49ers walk into that same city to face a new Magic King. Brian Flores’ bull is real. Minnesota’s front five weigh 1,391 pounds combined, about what a full-grown fighting bull weighs. And no defense in football has ever charged like this one: 72.5% of the time, per Next Gen Stats. Before this season, the record was 51.5%. But like any good magic trick, it’s built on getting you to watch the wrong hand. The big fellas inside aren’t the ones getting home. Minnesota’s interior linemen have combined to create pressure on just 6.4% of their rushes this season, per Sports Info Solutions, below the league average for a defensive tackle. Their best, Jalen Redmond, has 19 pressures on 257 rushes. Blake Cashman, a linebacker, has 24 on 88. That’s the trick. The danger is in the horns: Dallas Turner off the edge and Cashman walking up over the guards. And most of the time it’s five rushers, not six, with zone coverage sitting behind them. The Magic King doesn’t need everybody to come. He needs you to think everybody’s coming. The bull is young. The matador is not. The 49ers came into the year with one of the oldest rosters in the league, and Trent Williams, at 38, will spend Sunday night staring at a 23-year-old pass rusher. So the old matador goes back to the three words. Parar: Stand Still The young matador’s instinct is to drift back when the horns come. The old ones plant their feet. Offensive linemen have their own version of that. It’s called a jump set: instead of backing up and waiting for the rush, you meet the defender at the line, get your hands on him first and take away the runway before the charge ever builds. A blitzer who gets punched in the chest at the line of scrimmage can’t get where he’s going. This group has shown it can stand its ground. In Melbourne, Trent saw Myles Garrett one-on-one 11 times and gave up one pressure. And Brock Purdy doesn’t flinch either. When he’s been blitzed this year, he’s averaging 12.1 yards a throw with 12 touchdowns and two picks. Charging Brock Purdy has been an expensive habit. The horns are still real, and they’ll go looking for the youngest feet. Connor Colby has had his rough days, but almost all of them came against elite interior guys like Dallas’ Quinnen Williams, a technician you just can’t jump. Minnesota’s tackles aren’t that. Let Colby meet them at the line. The real question is whether Flores sends Blake Cashman right at him. If he does, Jake Brendel has to be the one sliding over to help, with Trent left alone on Turner. And if Cashman still gets through, the 49ers have a running back who ran into Quinnen Williams so hard on a bootleg that Williams left the game. An old matador can’t stand still for the young ones. But he can teach them where to plant their feet. Templar: Match The Charge Templar is the art of the cape, slowing the bull down to your rhythm until the charge belongs to you. For the 49ers, that’s the run game, and it’s where this whole line gets to go forward. Dominick Puni has the fewest blown run blocks of any 49ers lineman this season. Colton McKivitz is right behind him. Even Colby, a better run blocker than pass blocker, gets to go downhill and be himself. And it shows up every week. The 49ers are averaging 4.9 yards a carry this season against defenses that normally give up about 4.3. They’ve run better than a defense usually allows in six of nine games, including against the two best run defenses on the schedule, Seattle and the Rams. The other half of Templaris patience. In Dallas, the 49ers spent the first half dropping back and getting hit, five sacks on the night and a little bit of everything breaking down, and went into the locker room barely ahead. Shanahan didn’t panic. He stuck with the cape. In the second half, they ran it right at the Cowboys for 169 yards and scored 29 points. Minnesota’s bull charges upfield, and Turner rushes the passer on almost every passing down. Let him. Let him spend his fury on air while the ball goes through the space he just left. Teams that have shown that patience have made this defense sweat. Jonathan Taylor ran for 95 on them. Miami’s Ollie Gordon ripped off 86 yards on seven carries before the Dolphins apparently forgot he was on the roster. And when opponents run it 30 or more times, the Vikings are 2-2 and score 11.5 points a game. When they don’t, Minnesota is 5-0 and scores 26. Now, those were the old Vikings. Kirk Cousins is back, and he threw two touchdowns in his first game back. But Cousins doesn’t play defense. He doesn’t play running back, either. Minnesota has run for four touchdowns all season. He didn’t change the bull the 49ers have to face, only what’s at stake if they don’t tame it. Before, running the ball was how you beat this defense. Now it’s also how you keep Cousins and Justin Jefferson sitting on a bench in México City. Every carry drains a little more. The bull never notices. The crowd does. And the old matador knows exactly how many passes he has left. Mandar: Command It Mandar is what makes a matador a legend. Once the bull is held and slowed, he stops reacting and starts sending the charge exactly where he wants it. A bull charges what moves, and no offense in the NFL moves more before the snap than the 49ers. Motion is the flick of the cape. It makes the Magic King show his hand early. And when Purdy lines up under center, where Minnesota blitzes almost 90% of the time, the 49ers know exactly where the charge is headed. So send it somewhere, and go where it isn’t. When the rushers leave, they leave a hole in the zone behind them. That’s Christian McCaffrey’s grass. When Flores sends six or more, half of the big completions against him this year have gone to tight ends, and I don’t have to tell you who the 49ers’ tight end is. And then there’s Keenan Allen, 34, who has spent a career sitting down in the exact spot the blitzer just left and turning around to wave. A veteran who knows exactly where the bull just was? That’s the most matador thing on this roster. Minnesota’s corners are a different story. They haven’t allowed a touchdown all year. You don’t wave the cape in front of those horns. Unless Mike Evans is back, he hasn’t played since Oct. 19, and Kyle Shanahan is only “hoping” to get him on the practice field this week. But if he makes the trip, he’s the one guy you can throw to while the horns are still coming, and every safety Flores keeps back for him is one less body in the charge. The Bull’s Safe Spot Every bull has a querencia , the place in the ring where it feels strongest. Minnesota’s is third-and-long. Get there against a six-man rush, and you’re basically punting with extra steps. The matador’s job is to never let the bull get home: stay on schedule, keep it in the middle of the ring, and make it chase. They say a bull is never fought twice,…

title: Is this Kyle Shanahan’s best offense with the 49ers?
summary: Following a 46-point performance against the Dallas Cowboys, the San Francisco 49ers are 8-1 with the best record in the NFC halfway through the season. On Sunday, they weathered a rough defensive performance, responding every time with their offense to win a crucial game, as Brock Purdy had 389 yards and three touchdowns. San Francisco’s […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: George Kittle #85 of the San Francisco 49ers walks off the field after the game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following a 46-point performance against the Dallas Cowboys, the San Francisco 49ers are 8-1 with the best record in the NFC halfway through the season. On Sunday, they weathered a rough defensive performance, responding every time with their offense to win a crucial game, as Brock Purdy had 389 yards and three touchdowns. San Francisco’s offense has become hyper-efficient this year, as Purdy has enjoyed an MVP-caliber season, while the run game ranks in the top five in success rate and EPA per rush. This is the best quarterback play that Kyle Shanahan has had with the 49ers. He also might have his best true receiver since Julio Jones with Mike Evans (although 2021 Deebo Samuel and 2023 Brandon Aiyuk are both strong contenders). And the 49ers run game has returned to being efficient after an up-and-down 2025 season. Currently, the 49ers rank first in the NFL in yards per game and second in points per game. They’re balanced. They’re elite in the red zone. They’re first in the NFL in third-down conversion rate. Whatever the metric is, the 49ers offense seems to be near the top of the NFL this season. So, it’s a fair question to ask: is this Kyle Shanahan’s best offense with the 49ers? San Francisco just added another piece to the fold this past week, as Keenan Allen posted five catches for 61 yards in his 49ers debut. Now, on paper, the skill position group may not be as elite as the Brandon Aiyuk, Deebo Samuel, Jauan Jennings, George Kittle, and Christian McCaffrey group. But the 49ers have an elite WR1 in Mike Evans, quality complementary options with Deebo Samuel, Keenan Allen, and (eventually) De’Zhaun Stribling, and Kittle and McCaffrey still in the fold. Their banged-up group still posted nearly 500 yards of offense on Sunday against the Dallas Cowboys, and Kittle has high hopes for the rest of the season. “When you add Mike Evans to [our current offense], I’ve actually never been more confident in an offense,” the star tight end said on Sunday. And it’s a fair assessment. The 49ers have a go-to receiver. They have strong yards-after-the-catch weapons with Samuel, Kittle, and McCaffrey. They just added a very good separator with Keenan Allen. And they have a quality offensive line that has been a good unit in both pass protection and run blocking. Now, the one true knock is age. All of the 49ers top weapons are 30+ years old, and we’ve already seen the injury bug hit this season. But fully healthy? This very well could be Kyle Shanahan’s best offense as the 49ers head coach. The last moving part is Shanahan himself. He’s put himself firmly in the Coach of the Year mix and just continues to elevate as a playcaller and play designer. The biggest test of the season comes next weekend against the formidable Minnesota Vikings defense. If San Francisco is able to even thwart Brian Flores’s elite group, then there’s no doubt this is an offense to be reckoned with this season.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: How ‘backyard football’ play style has contributed to Brock Purdy’s MVP like campaign
summary: It’s no secret that San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy is enjoying the best season of his career this year, as he’s been considered in the MVP conversation once again amongst several elite quarterbacks in the NFL. Thus far, Purdy has thrown for 2,369 yards, 20 touchdowns, and five interceptions, while completing a career-high 70.1 […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers looks to pass during the second half against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret that San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy is enjoying the best season of his career this year, as he’s been considered in the MVP conversation once again amongst several elite quarterbacks in the NFL. Thus far, Purdy has thrown for 2,369 yards, 20 touchdowns, and five interceptions, while completing a career-high 70.1 percent of his passes. The yards per attempt (9.0) remains high, while his QBR (81.3) ranks second in the NFL. Purdy had one of his best games of the season in San Francisco’s thriller victory this past weekend, completing 22 of 28 passes for 389 yards and three touchdowns. It was a big improvisational day, as Purdy was able to extend plays and make key throws on his feet, with the most impressive being one of Christian McCaffrey’s long catch-and-run touchdowns after Purdy created time rolling to his right. “I’m always trying to keep my eyes down the field when I’m scrambling and stuff, and seeing if guys can feel me and see me, and try to get to space,” Purdy said of the play. “But then there’s a point where it’s like, ‘All right, I think I can try to go use my legs now in this moment.’ And I was going to do that, and then all of a sudden, I just felt Christian pop. So I stopped and gave him the ball, and I was probably right at the line of scrimmage, so it was pretty close.” Well, McCaffrey attributed it to ‘backyard football’, which kind of feels exactly how Purdy has played at several times this year. “It really is backyard football at that point,” the star running back added said. “I think we’ve all played it as kids at recess when you’re drawing up plays on your hand and then it never happens. You ever tell a five-year-old to run like a post route, and he just runs a corner or something else, but he’s open? That was kind of what that was. And again, I think those little decisions that you make in games for Brock to not scramble, not to just surrender the play, but to keep it alive, that’s a big deal. So there’s no planning that goes into that. It’s just him doing a great job playing ball.” Purdy has made a number of impressive improvisational plays that show off both his IQ and playmaking ability, adding yet another layer to a 49ers offense that has already been clicking on all cylinders. It’s not just that Purdy is making these ‘backyard football’ type of throws; he’s doing so consistently while keeping the ball out of harm’s way and playing with a changing set of pass-catchers. It feels like the final piece of the puzzle, making him a truly complete quarterback, which has now shown up on film all year long. We’ve seen other MVP candidates like Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes, and even Joe Burrow at times make the backyard football-like plays to extend drives for their teams. Purdy has started to ascend into that group this year with a variety of plays that should keep him in the MVP discussion if he keeps up his current style of play.

title: Should the 49ers have challenged the fumble call?
summary: So while we’re talking about how bad the defense was and how great the offense was in the San Francisco 49ers’ 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys, there’s still one thing to bring up: the officiating. It was terrible. Not like you can expect much more from a crew ran by John Hussey. Sorry to […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 15: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner celebrates during the NFL game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Dallas Cowboys on November 15, 2026 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images So while we’re talking about how bad the defense was and how great the offense was in the San Francisco 49ers’ 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys, there’s still one thing to bring up: the officiating. It was terrible. Not like you can expect much more from a crew ran by John Hussey . Sorry to say, it probably wasn’t going to get much better, because if the 49ers didn’t get Hussey, they would have gotten Bill Vinovich . You can call one the lesser of the two evils, but it’s still evil. And don’t say we didn’t see it coming: Buckle up, #49ers ’ fans. https://t.co/iCVbKtWVKt — Bonta Hill (@BontaHill) November 15, 2026 And Hussey did just about what you’d expect from Hussey. But the league will want you to celebrate him for going down the street to make this game with a crew that hasn’t worked together. That will probably also be the excuse—if we ever get one (don’t count on it). Because after all, Hussey had to go to this game after all the air traffic control issues over the weekend. So he saved the day. What a hero. Whatever. Before we go any further, it’s important to note that officiating would NOT have been the reason the 49ers lost yesterday, even if it had happened. Dre Greenlaw not catching a gift interception would be why they lost. The lack of a pass rush would be why they lost. Deommodore Lenoir getting diced just as much as he was defending passes would be why they lost. In fact, no need to be so granular. The defense would be why they lost. But the two aren’t mutually exclusive, and Hussey’s inconsistencies put the defense in a tougher spot. We can go on and on about how badly that game was officiated. Some calls will get arguments; others won’t. For instance, Osa Odighizuwa got flagged early in the game for roughing the passer. Niners flagged for roughing the passer on Dak Prescott pic.twitter.com/8zmSDHGFsP — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) November 15, 2026 That’s a battle I’m not going to engage in. The call can go either way. It is the rules, and it looks like body weight. You can argue that he was braced with a free hand, but in real time? I’m not going to fault the crew for that one. I will fault them for Brock Purdy taking a headshot later in the game after throwing the ball. Anytime the head moves from the QB after throwing the ball, it’s a roughing penalty. But not for Hussey and Brock Purdy. I tried to find video but couldn’t. There’s also the blatant pass interference that was very one-sided. Here’s a good example: No pass interference? pic.twitter.com/TSuksyL7zY — Coach Yac 🗣 (@Coach_Yac) November 15, 2026 If you’re going to do that, make sure you’re consistent. With this crew that’s asking an awful lot. Let’s move onto this gem of a phantom penalty: The NFL has become an absolute joke! That hit by 49ers safety Malik Mustapha was a textbook football tackle! Right in the chest, delivering a hard, clean hit trying to jar the football loose. That’s exactly how you’re taught to play the game! What the hell is a defensive player… pic.twitter.com/HPlVKZBW0h — Dan Coccimiglio (@NorCalSportsNW) November 16, 2026 Huh? What, and I want a lot of dots after this because this is important…………… What the hell is that? I can understand a flag in the moment due to speed, but how does replay not remove that foul? How does the discussion during the ref show go on for this and no one can speak up to say “didn’t look violent.” Instead, a great play gets wiped, and a player is kicked for doing their job. I don’t know what’s more inconsistent, Hussey or the replay assist. None of those calls are really surprising. What is surprising is this: That’s a fumble Dallas scored on this drive by the way… 😡 https://t.co/Hcip2YxtYr pic.twitter.com/zdTFxglHAS — Coach Yac 🗣 (@Coach_Yac) November 15, 2026 Ladies and gentlemen, that is a fumble. Was it recovered? Nope. Was it even reviewed? Nope. Was there even a chance to have a recovery? Nope. And this is where I wonder who is more at fault: Hussey or Kyle Shanahan. For a coach with some head-scratching challenges over the years. This no-challenge might be one of the more head-scratching ones of all. Or is it? “We knew it was out,” Shanahan said in his post-game press conference. “That’s why I wanted to throw it [the challenge flag]. And I thought that we did have it, but somehow, a guy on their team was walking away with the ball.” For the turnover to happen, the film has to show a clear recovery by the 49ers. While Shanahan thought Malik Mustapha recovered the ball, his analysts upstairs and the scene of the 49ers not walking away with the ball were enough for him to put the flag back into his pocket. But if Mustapha had it, why did the Cowboys walk away with it? “The refs were telling us to get up and stop fighting for it,” Fred Warner said, recalling the play. “Because they had the ball, and I was trying to fight. But I also didn’t want to get a penalty for trying to delay the game” Makes sense. Here’s the play in question . Now, from the angle on the broadcast, I don’t know where the ball is in relation to the whistles—but that leads to my next question: why were the whistles blown? How did a referee not see that, and why was the beanbag thrown down? Why are they not fighting for control of the ball? Why is this not being reviewed anyway? How did this get so mucked up? So if there’s no clear recovery—fine, that is understood, but the whistle shouldn’t have been blown in the first place until after they started untangling the pile and telling everyone to let go. At least, that’s how it looks from my point of view. Truthfully, we won’t know who recovered the ball, but it could have been worth a challenge anyway. Given what we know, it’s doubtful the 49ers would have won the challenge, but it would have been worthwhile one, I suppose. It really shouldn’t have gotten to that point. Hussey’s crew should have seen the ball pop out and/or let the fumble and subsequent recovery happen. But that’s not how they operate. Because of reasons. Knowing what you know, would you have thrown the challenge flag anyway, or would you have held off, knowing that it was a losing battle?

title: Reviewing Keenan Allen’s first game with the 49ers
summary: When the San Francisco 49ers sent a sixth-round pick for veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen, the thoughts of the experienced receiver moving the chains and shaking free in a phone booth ran wild. Sunday was Allen’s first action with the 49ers and only 21 snaps; his impact was felt, and if his first action is […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 15: San (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When the San Francisco 49ers sent a sixth-round pick for veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen, the thoughts of the experienced receiver moving the chains and shaking free in a phone booth ran wild. Sunday was Allen’s first action with the 49ers and only 21 snaps; his impact was felt, and if his first action is an indicator, then the best is yet to come for the former Cal receiver. Allen was targeted seven times and hauled in five passes for 61 yards with eight snaps in the slot and 13 outside. The YAC number is low at only 2.0 per reception, but his 12.2 yards per catch average is in line with a player who understands where he needs to be as a reliable target. In fact, four of his five catches were first downs. That is literally the type of player the 49ers needed and traded for. The left side of the formation was where Allen did his most damage, with one catch over 20-plus yards for 23 yards and an intermediate grab in the ten to 20-yard range for 14 yards. The timing of those routes was on full display with Brock Purdy, and the connection was immediate. Facing Daron Bland and Cobie Durant on the outside led to 28 yards on three catches. In a fun twist by defensive coordinator Christian Parker, Allen was lined up on Von Miller and caught his lone target for ten yards. I have to say Parker is a forward-thinking football mind, because nobody would ever put Miller in coverage. Against Caleb Downs, Allen caught one pass for 23 yards. With the potential return of Mike Evans for Sunday night against Minnesota, Allen will have more space to operate, with another week under his belt and having faced the Vikings once this season, which can provide valuable insight into creating explosives for the passing game. The Vikings will be aggressive as usual, but the experience of Evans and Allen will be a very tough challenge for Brian Flores and his defense. This week will be exciting, with Evans, Allen, and Deebo Samuel all being mixed in as weapons. The acquisition of Allen is already providing dividends, and the best is yet to come from the veteran in this offense. Let the “unction” continue!

title: What midseason 49ers trends matter?
summary: Through ten weeks, the San Francisco 49ers are 8-1, with their two most difficult matchups of the season in Mexico City against Minnesota and at home against the Seahawks upcoming. With eight games remaining, this feels like the halfway point of the season for the 49ers and a large enough sample size to analyze certain […]
full_text: (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through ten weeks, the San Francisco 49ers are 8-1, with their two most difficult matchups of the season in Mexico City against Minnesota and at home against the Seahawks upcoming. With eight games remaining, this feels like the halfway point of the season for the 49ers and a large enough sample size to analyze certain trends and tendencies. Which trends will continue, and which have a chance to change? Brock Purdy’s numbers against the blitz This trend matters because of Brian Flores and the Vikings defense. The 49ers offense won’t be able to use play action, since turning your back to the coverages is as difficult as it gets when the coverage changes. Expect a ton of straight dropbacks from under center to give Brock Purdy a chance to decipher the coverages. Against the blitz, Purdy has punished opposing defenses to the tune of +0.33 EPA/dropback on 86 blitzed dropbacks. Flores will turn the heat up, but the simulated pressures will be something to watch as the defensive coordinator plays on your expectations and could just send four and drop four more, or any other variation you can think of. This number matters as teams are looking for any way to slow down this 49ers offense. The 49ers defense in expected passing situations Look, Sunday was rough on defense, in particular the secondary. The Cowboys did what they wanted all Sunday. Surprisingly, the 49ers are eighth in the NFL in expected passing situations, allowing a -0.13 EPA/dropback. Expected passing situations are defined as 70% based on down, distance, score, time left, etc. The 49ers under Raheem Morris are a Cover 3 defense with a 48% C3 rate in expected passing situations. The second-highest defensive coverage is Cover 1 Man at 16.6%. The 49ers will have to pressure Kirk Cousins on Sunday night. Speaking of… The 49ers’ pass rush At first glance, it felt like the 49ers’ pass rush was nonexistent. After a rewatch, I don’t hold that same opinion. The Cowboys dropped back trying to keep up, and the 49ers generated 26 pressures, two sacks (one negated by a penalty), 12 QB hits, and 12 hurries. Mykel Williams had an effective game, as did Keion White and Nick Bosa. White finished with a 30.8% pass-rush win rate in true pass sets, and Bosa was second at 29.4%. Pressuring Cousins will lead to turnover chances for the 49ers’ defense, but the pass rush is on the cusp of a huge game.

title: The 49ers are ‘hoping’ Mike Evans returns to practice, but it’s ‘still too early’ to tell
summary: The only injury the San Francisco 49ers had in Week 10 was cornerback Renardo Green’s back injury. Kyle Shanahan said Green is day-to-day, and the team will further assess him on Wednesday. The big injury update we’re all awaiting is about Mike Evans. Shanahan was asked whether Evans would return to practice this week. He […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The only injury the San Francisco 49ers had in Week 10 was cornerback Renardo Green’s back injury. Kyle Shanahan said Green is day-to-day, and the team will further assess him on Wednesday. The big injury update we’re all awaiting is about Mike Evans. Shanahan was asked whether Evans would return to practice this week. He said, “I’m hoping to, just not sure yet. Still too early. He’s flying tonight with the guys who are left behind, who didn’t travel with us to Dallas. So, we’ll see how these next few days go and see if he can get out there sometime this week.” Evans has missed the previous three games. The 49ers have one loss during that stretch, but you can’t pin that on Evans. That was a turnover-filled game for the Niners. The offense moved the ball up and down the field against Atlanta. The same was true against the Raiders and the Cowboys, but those are two of the league’s worst defenses. When it counts, like against the Vikings and Seahawks, the Niners will need their WR1. ESPN spoke with Dr. Daniel Kaplan, an orthopedic surgeon, to further clarify Evans’ Achilles injury and everything he’s dealing with. Here’s what Kaplan said about the recovery timeline: It totally depends on the severity. Also, timing in the season. If it’s like the Super Bowl, he’s playing because it’s mostly about a pain thing as opposed to necessarily a function aspect. We usually assume it’s in the two- to four-week range for tendinitis. That’s about what I would expect. Longer than that sometimes, but a lot of it has to do with how much he’s actually shut down. It sounds like they did the right thing by actually shutting him down, as opposed to the other option is trying to play through it and letting it drag on and then it’s just never going to resolve. This week marks a month since Evans last stepped foot on a football field. By Week 11, it’ll be outside the four-week period. Kaplan discussed how you are still actively treating the injury, and it’s not, “Don’t play for three weeks and you’ll be fine.” Kaplan said there’s no risk of rupture. The concern is that Evans could sustain the same injury once he returns. Here’s what Kaplan had to say about the possibility of Evans aggravating the injury: Mostly just depending on usage. Now, if he’s prone to it for some sort of biomechanical reason, I suppose it’s possible. But to my knowledge, it’s not like that’s something that he has been battling over the course of his career. So, I don’t think so as long as it does resolve. And that’s where the secret sauce comes in about really determining when it’s safe for him to go back because you obviously don’t want to keep him out any longer than you have to. But if you send him back too soon, then you restart the clock and now all of a sudden, it’s another two weeks here, another week there. It’s kind of like when people have hamstring tears and you follow those; it’s the same idea. Being overly cautious might make the most sense, especially given where the 49ers are in the current playoff picture .

title: NFL power rankings: Not everybody is sold on the 49ers being No. 1
summary: It’s Tuesday, which means we’ll show the NFL power rankings from around the league, and some thoughts about the San Francisco 49ers. ESPN Week 10 result: Beat the Cowboys 46-40Week 10 ranking: 2 Non-QB MVP at midseason: LB Fred Warner While QB Brock Purdy is a top candidate for league MVP, Warner is making a […]
full_text: (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It’s Tuesday, which means we’ll show the NFL power rankings from around the league, and some thoughts about the San Francisco 49ers. ESPN Week 10 result: Beat the Cowboys 46-40 Week 10 ranking: 2 Non-QB MVP at midseason: LB Fred Warner While QB Brock Purdy is a top candidate for league MVP , Warner is making a strong case to be the first linebacker to win Defensive Player of the Year since Luke Kuechly in 2013. Warner’s 88 tackles rank sixth in the NFL. He’s tied for first in forced fumbles (five) to go with a fumble recovery, 0.5 sacks and three pass breakups. He has done all that after returning from a broken and dislocated right ankle injury that cost him most of last season. For a defense on its fifth coordinator in five years, Warner is the constant and one of the primary reasons the Niners are 8-1. — Nick Wagoner The Athletic 2. San Francisco 49ers (8-1) Last week: 2 Sunday: Beat Cowboys 46-40 Breakout player: Renardo Green The third-year cornerback had a tough day on Sunday against George Pickens and company, but he was dealing with a back injury and had already built up plenty of goodwill this year. Green, a second-round pick in 2024, has four interceptions, three more than he had in his first two seasons combined. Rookie running back Kaelon Black has also been a surprise with 356 rushing yards behind Christian McCaffrey. NFL Did I expect San Francisco to give up 40 points to the Cowboys? No, I foresaw them surrendering just 20, in fact. Does that concern me much? No, not really. The 49ers won a wild shootout in Arlington by staying true to themselves offensively — crafting a beautiful blend of creative play-calling with artistic improvisation from Brock Purdy to light up Dallas’ beleaguered defense — and they did enough defensively to get the job done. Nick Bosa isn’t quite making the impact I’d hoped to see in his return from injury, but it’s still early in that process and the defense remains a strong group overall. Until proven otherwise, this is the NFL’s best squad. Bleacher report 2. San Francisco 49ers Last Week: 2 Week 10 Result: Won at Dallas 46-40 The San Francisco 49ers continue to look like the best team in the NFC, though they did have some hiccups against the Cowboys on Sunday. Brock Purdy had another MVP-caliber outing, as Christian McCaffrey, Deebo Samuel, and other 49ers playmakers repeatedly knifed through Dallas’ suspect defense. The deadline trade for receiver Keenan Allen paid immediate dividends, and it’s fun to think about how potent the offense could be once Allen is fully integrated into the game plan and Mike Evans is healthy again. However, San Francisco’s pass rush continues to underwhelm, and its defense struggled overall in Dallas. Next week’s matchup with the Kirk Cousins-led Vikings will be a massive test. Yahoo Sports 2. San Francisco 49ers (8-1, LW: 2) The 49ers cooked the Cowboys’ defense , putting up 46 points and 584 yards. Dallas’ defense is dreadful but it’s still hard to pile up close to 600 yards in any NFL game. The way the 49ers have climbed to the top of the NFL in yards per game is worth studying. Brock Purdy was famously Mr. Irrelevant in the draft and now he’s an MVP candidate. Christian McCaffrey was at a point in which age and touches should have started to chip away at his effectiveness, but he is tied for the NFL lead with 13 total touchdowns. Draft experts laughed at the Kaelon Black pick in the third round; he’s one of the best backup running backs in the league. Deebo Samuel Sr.’s career looked like it might be over after last season, but he has five touchdowns in six games. The 49ers had to give up only a sixth-round draft pick for Keenan Allen in a trade and he had five catches for 61 yards on Sunday. The conclusion: Kyle Shanahan is your NFL Coach of the Year. USA TODAY 1. San Francisco 49ers (1): The defensive performance wasn’t all that inspiring Sunday, but the Niners are re-incorporating players on that side of the ball. They’re still not completely whole on offense, either, WRs Mike Evans and De’Zhaun Stribling the most notable absentees right now. But when you’re averaging 9.4 yards per play anyway, then you’re a pretty dangerous operation − maybe a Super one, though the upcoming matchups with Minnesota and Seattle will be much truer litmus tests than Dallas was. FOX Sports Super Bowl odds: +500 (tied for the best) The 49ers put on some offensive show in Dallas, running up 584 yards and scoring six touchdowns against the Cowboys. Then again, given how soft the Dallas defense has been this season, maybe that’s not as impressive as it sounds. Besides, everyone knew the 49ers were explosive on offense. We all just thought they were better on defense. They were torn apart for 343 yards and five touchdown passes by Dak Prescott , who kept getting the Cowboys back into striking distance of a miracle comeback. If Dallas’ defense was even mediocre, with the ability to make just one more stop, the 49ers would have lost. Next game: vs. Vikings (Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET) Stat To Know : The 49ers averaged 9.4 yards per play against the Cowboys, the most by any team in a game over the past two seasons. They also scored three touchdowns of 60-plus yards from scrimmage, tying the most by any team in a game over the past 50 years.

title: Kyle Shanahan on 49ers’ defensive effort in Dallas: ‘The tape tells a different story’
summary: For the 49ers’ defense following San Francisco’s shootout victory over the Dallas Cowboys, the mood in the locker room was anything but celebratory. Having forced five turnovers in the Week 9 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, Week 10 saw the defense endure its most significant struggles of the season, giving up five touchdowns in […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 15: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner celebrates during the NFL game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Dallas Cowboys on November 15, 2026 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For the 49ers’ defense following San Francisco’s shootout victory over the Dallas Cowboys, the mood in the locker room was anything but celebratory. Having forced five turnovers in the Week 9 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, Week 10 saw the defense endure its most significant struggles of the season, giving up five touchdowns in San Francisco’s 46-40 win. The 49ers had issues getting home on pass rushes, recording only one sack of Dak Prescott, which was split between Mykel Williams and Dre Greenlaw, while a banged-up secondary struggled to contain wideout George Pickens. As such, there was plenty of frustration among the 49er defenders following the display Raheem Morris’ unit put on the field, which was articulated by defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. “Not every win is going to be perfect, and we found a way to win [against Dallas],” Buckner told reporters. “The offense, we had to lean on the offense heavily; we needed 46 to win the game, and they put up 46… We just got to execute all four quarters, though. “We didn’t do that, and we know that’s why the win feels kind of like a loss to a bunch of us [and] we just got to continue to get better. It’s not the lack of locking in. I feel like guys are like that. It’s just executing each and every play to the best of our abilities, and we’re not doing that on a consistent basis.” While that mindset is of no surprise to Kyle Shanahan, the 49ers head coach was keen to put the defense’s efforts in perspective when asked about the win feeling like a loss on that side of the ball. Shanahan told his Monday conference call: “That’s how I expect them to [approach it]. Anytime you come off a field and that’s what the stats say, you’re not going to feel good about yourself. I think the tape tells a little bit of a different story. I didn’t think it was like that for three quarters and I think we kind of fell apart defensively in the fourth quarter, which made it very bad. That’s why you’ve got to put it in perspective. No, it wasn’t good and we can clean a lot of that stuff up and do better and we expect to. I felt pretty similar in the offensive standpoint, just the opposite way. If you look at the stats and the scoreboard and everything, it seems like the offense played one of their best games ever, but I didn’t feel that way at all. I thought we had three big plays that were really good by all our guys, but I think you take those three plays away and there’s a lot of stuff that we could have cleaned up and done better on offense.” He added: “It’s a week-to-week league and really excited for that win. Never going to take that away from those guys. Even look at special teams. I thought special teams had a really good chance to really affect that game. They held a good returner in check. I thought we got some explosive returns, but we ruined them with some dumb penalties. Some stuff that we could overcome. I think we left about 70 yards out there taken back or given collectively on special teams with penalties. “Really all three phases, it was kind of a crazy game where things just stat-wise they stuck out a ton. But, there’s a lot to learn from that silent tape and not to get too caught up in it either way, good or bad.” Shanahan has long since preached the value of not getting too high after a win, and not getting too low following a defeat. While a game that saw the defense concede 40 may feel like a disaster for those on that side of the ball, Shanahan is right to stress that there were positives. San Francisco forced two Dallas punts in the second quarter that allowed the 49ers to go into the half with a one-point lead, before the Niners in success in holding the Cowboys to a field goal on their first possession of the half and then forcing a turnover on their next series helped enable the offense to stretch the advantage to 19. As Shanahan mentioned, a key problem for the 49er defense is that it appeared to completely run out of gas in the fourth quarter, when Dallas scored three touchdowns to keep the game competitive right until the end. Avoiding that happening again will be critical for the Niners in Week 11 as they face the Minnesota Vikings at altitude in Mexico City in Week 11 in what projects as a massive game for seeding in the NFC playoffs. But one disappointing performance doesn’t change the fact the defense has made clear progress in 2026. For the 49ers to achieve their goal and end the postseason with the Lombardi in hand, they will need to get the pass rush going down the stretch and in the playoffs. The good news is the 49ers have the talent and the time still on their side to make those strides that could see the entire locker room enjoy the biggest of celebrations come February.

title: How the Titans should align at WR vs. Cowboys in Week 11
summary: The Tennessee Titans will have some decisions to make at wide receiver versus the Dallas Cowboys this week. Rookie stud Carnell Tate is returning to practice and is expected to be in the lineup. We’ve examined how Brian Daboll should utilize his receivers against the Cowboys in Week 11. Carnell Tate It goes without saying […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Carnell Tate #14 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans will have some decisions to make at wide receiver versus the Dallas Cowboys this week . Rookie stud Carnell Tate is returning to practice and is expected to be in the lineup. We’ve examined how Brian Daboll should utilize his receivers against the Cowboys in Week 11. Carnell Tate It goes without saying that Tate should reclaim his spot as WR1 in the lineup. His two-game absence means he’s only played one game alongside Cam Ward since the Titans made the philosophical shift to a more aggressive no-huddle offense . Ward has caught fire, and having Tate back at his disposal should be a terrific development for a passing game starting to find its footing. Elic Ayomanor Elic Ayomanor had a frustrating and inconsistent day versus the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 10, but he still registered five receptions for a team-high 79 yards. That included an explosive 50-yard pass from Ward. Ayomanor is currently the Titans’ 2nd-most consistent receiver. He can move around the offensive formation, but is best suited to play on the outside. Chimere Dike Wan’Dale Robinson was placed on IR with an ankle injury . The Titans seemingly benched Calvin Ridley, who was limited to seven snaps versus the Jaguars. With Robinson sidelined, Xavier Restrepo was promoted to the roster. Chimere Dike deserves to be receiving opportunities in the slot, with Restrepo and Ridley mixing in. Dike had 71 receiving yards and a touchdown versus the Bengals two weeks ago, and should be getting extended looks at receiver with the two veteran options struggling. He’s capable of playing more snaps.

title: Commanders LB Sonny Styles’ processing power makes him more dangerous
summary: The New York Giants faced a third-and-3 coming out of the two-minute warning, needing to move the sticks to maintain a slim lead and possession of the ball.   Commanders linebacker Sonny Styles understood that situation. His quarterback had thrown interceptions on consecutive series leading up to this moment, and Washington needed to give Jayden […]
full_text: The New York Giants faced a third-and-3 coming out of the two-minute warning, needing to move the sticks to maintain a slim lead and possession of the ball. Commanders linebacker Sonny Styles understood that situation. His quarterback had thrown interceptions on consecutive series leading up to this moment, and Washington needed to give Jayden Daniels one more shot to go win it. The stakes didn’t change Styles’ approach to crucial play. The Ohio State product diagnosed it appropriately, sensed what was coming and used freak athleticism to make the defensive play of the day. “Last time we played them and we had a third-and-4 situation around midfield and they had a crack toss to the back,” Styles said. “When they went empty, just looking at the tight end, it looked like he was cracking. Charles said something like that, too, so I thought it was going to be a QB run. I just reacted.” He reacted well in a play you’ve certainly seen a bunch by now. Sonny Styles said absolutely not on 3rd down. WASvsNYG on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/1d9S7zwsT3 — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 “Everyone understood that we had to get a stop right there,” Styles said. “Guys bowed up.” Washington got the ball back and Daniels rewarded that effort with a decisive, 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs. That play will lead the highlights from a 24-21 victory over the Giants that essentially saved Washington’s season. None of that happens without Styles and an overall defensive effort where Washington’s foot never left the gas. This wasn’t a singular event. The No. 7 overall NFL draft pick has been a marvel in this early season, and not solely due to insane athleticism. He’s a smart player who can read offenses well and make plays on the ball. While he’s far from perfect and with room for improvement, his first nine game qualify as an excellent start to his NFL career. Styles has 80 tackles and the season’s just nine games deep. While number of tackles isn’t the important stat that it used to be, that’s still a sign that Styles is doing things right. Jeremy Reaves’ 55 is the next highest total on Washington’s defense. The rookie, Styles, has had 13 tackles in four of the past five games. Sonny Styles had exactly 13 tackles in four of his last five games. That included 26 in the span of four days between the Rams and Giants Just like at Ohio State, he's grown during the year without needing to wait for the offseason #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/3tGxtjN10b — Grant Mitchell (@FullCommandShow) November 18, 2026 He has validated GM Adam Peters’ decision to draft a non-premium position at No. 7 . The dude can play. Styles was critical of some plays, including some hesitance as a blitzer, which is keeping him a step behind. His stat line , overall: 80 tackles, including five for a loss, a sack, and interception, four passes defensed and four quarterback pressures in 46 blitzes. He has allowed 30 catches for 288 yards and a touchdown on 45 targets, for an 82.5 passer rating allowed. The Commanders will need him leading the defensive surge toward the better play and consistent wins that are required for a real turnaround. The scary part about Styles is that his athleticism will get more effective as he takes more snaps and processes information faster. He’s the primary reason for hope and the long-term success on defense, assuming, of course, that the front office can surround him with talent in ways they haven’t quite done for Daniels. That’s a discussion for the offseason. Styles and the Commanders will continue competing for the NFC East title down the stretch, with that Week 10 win against the Giants as a possible pivot point. “This win isn’t going to turn the whole season,” Styles said. “We have to keep working, keep pushing and get getting better.”

title: Commanders News: Keeping pace with Bengals QB Joe Burrow no easy task

full_text: The Daily Slop Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room Commanders Film Review: Ben Sinnott vs Giants It’s fair to say Commanders tight end Ben Sinnott has yet to live up to the lofty expectations of being a second round pick back in 2024. Sinnott has quietly developed into a strong blocker that can line up as a tight end or move around into fullback positions, so he still provides some value to the team, but his receiving numbers have been almost nonexistent. Prior to the Giants game on Thursday night, Sinnott had a total of 17 catches for 148 yards and two touchdowns through the first two and a half years of his career. Obviously, much more production is expected from a second round pick. But against the Giants, Sinnott had the best game of his career to date. When starting tight end Chig Okonkwo left the game with an injury, Sinnott stepped up and caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown. Again, those aren’t staggering numbers, but they were career high numbers for a player that has lacked opportunities and production in the passing game. So let’s dive into Sinnott’s career day and see what might be sustainable going forward. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE SI.com Can the Commanders Keep Pace With Joe Burrow Without Terry McLaurin? A month after tying the Giants, the Washington Commanders beat them 24–21 Thursday night and kept their season alive. Monday brings a familiar quarterback in Joe Burrow. Jayden Daniels beat him and the Bengals 38–33 in 2024. Now Washington faces the prospect of keeping pace with Burrow without Terry McLaurin. What Changed Since the 2024 Shootout Daniels, in just his third career game, began his iconic rookie-year scoring reel in Cincinnati, at a time when the Bengals were still respected as one of the NFL’s feared contenders. His 27-yard pass to lead wideout Terry McLaurin was one of the most electrifying instances of the stars’ immediate chemistry, as well as one of the first indicators of the potentially special underdog roster that Washington’s executives had compiled. McLaurin caught four passes for 100 yards against Cincinnati in 2024. He’s out for the season after tearing his patellar tendon. Stefon Diggs caught the winning 32-yard touchdown against the Giants last week, and Antonio Williams scored from 31 yards out. If Monday requires the same kind of scoring from Daniels, those are plays Washington needs from its current receivers. Cincinnati’s defensive front looks different from the one Daniels faced in 2024. After Trey Hendrickson’s departure, Boye Mafe became a primary edge rusher, while Dexter Lawrence and former Commander Jonathan Allen added strength inside. Cincinnati’s defense gave up 36 points to Tennessee on November 1, so Daniels should have chances. The Bengals have since beaten Atlanta and Pittsburgh, holding the Steelers to 18 points Sunday while Burrow threw for 409 yards and four touchdowns . Cincinnati is 7–2 and has won five straight. Washington may need far more than it scored against the Giants to keep up Monday. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Download the SB Nation app Commanders fans, take command of game day! Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Chat live during every game Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Commanders.com ‘Baby Kobe’: Jayden Daniels was clutch when Commanders needed him most Jayden Daniels, who was the only starting quarterback not to throw an interception heading into the Washington Commanders’ second matchup with the New York Giants, opened his postgame press conference with a joke. “Yes, I threw two picks,” Daniels said. “Yeah, got that out of my system. So, we can move forward about that.” Daniels delivered a clutch performance — his first fourth-quarter comeback in almost two seasons — against the Giants, finding Stefon Diggs for a 32-yard touchdown to give the Commanders a 24-21 victory. However, what he did on the previous two drives played a role in making the moment necessary, as he threw two interceptions in a span of five plays. Each moment felt like a death knell for the Commanders, who needed a win in Week 10 to keep their playoff hopes — and their season — alive. But if the interceptions were proof that Daniels is still a young quarterback with plenty to learn, the plays he made with the game on the line were the latest examples of why he’s viewed as the future of the franchise. “I was proud of him [Daniels] for coming back to respond and ripping it,” head coach Dan Quinn said after the game. Daniels had put together a solid game through the first three quarters. He looked comfortable in the pocket as he led the offense to 17 points, throwing his ninth and 10th touchdowns of the season to Ben Sinnott and Antonio Williams, respectively. There were some bumps along the way, like taking a sack for a 14-yard loss and failing to capitalize on a forced fumble from the defense, but Daniels looked mostly like himself, completing 16 of his 21 pass attempts for 180 yards in the first 45 minutes. The Commanders’ next three drives ended in frustration at best and disaster at worst. They stalled on fourth-and-1 at the Giants’ 30-yard line, setting up a 66-yard touchdown from Isaiah Likely that gave New York a four-point lead three plays later. The Commanders got into Giants’ territory again, but Daniels’s pass to Chig Okonkwo was underthrown and thrown inside, which made it easy for safety Javon Holland to intercept it at the Giants’ 2-yard line. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Laremy Tunsil’s next step leaves Commanders facing more than a medical call Head coach Dan Quinn confirmed that left tackle Laremy Tunsil has moved on to the next stage of his rehabilitation from a torn triceps after a recent doctor’s visit. It’s the strength part of the process, but the Washington Commanders still don’t know if he will feature again in 2026. It’s a precarious situation, but the Commanders shouldn’t rush things. And Tunsil’s return may even be predicated on how the Commanders fare heading into their stretch run. Laremy Tunsil’s recovery takes the next step, but Commanders should be cautious Losing the five-time Pro Bowl blindside enforcer during training camp was a body blow. Tunsil is one of the few elite players Washington has, arguably the team’s best overall player. And his presence has been sorely missed. Brandon Coleman is trying to fill the void , but his skills look best suited to the interior. There isn’t really anybody else who can man the left tackle spot, aside from Esa Pole on the practice squad. That speaks to a lack of depth and the wrong offseason recruitment approach, but it shouldn’t impact Washington’s plan with Tunsil. Tunsil’s been out for months. He may be making good progress, but until his strength returns, the Commanders’ hands are tied. And if they are out of contention in the coming weeks, one has to wonder what the point of Tunsil’s return would be. Obviously, Tunsil is a supreme competitor. Even in his absence, the Ole Miss product has stayed engaged, helping the likes of Coleman and right tackle Josh Conerly Jr. with their technique, overall approach, and week-to-week preparation. That’s a sign of his exceptional leadership , but he will no doubt be itching to get back onto the field. A win over the Bengals on Monday night would shoot them up the rankings, while a loss can still get washed away by facing an offensive juggernaut led by the MVP-favorite this season.
